Commission
The Commission is an authority that the scientific panel can request documentation or information from regarding AI provider activities.<SEP>The Commission is an entity responsible for developing and recommending model contractual terms for high-risk AI systems, facilitating cooperation in the value chain.<SEP>The Commission, commonly known as the European Commission, serves as the executive branch of the European Union (EU) and is entrusted with a wide array of critical responsibilities. It plays a pivotal role in proposing legislation, implementing decisions made by the EU Parliament and the Council, and upholding the EU treaties. The Commission works in conjunction with the Advisory Forum to ensure stakeholder representation, enhancing its regulatory effectiveness.

Among its numerous duties, the Commission focuses significantly on technology and artificial intelligence (AI). It is responsible for adopting implementing acts and codes of practice related to content regulation, ensuring compliance with obligations surrounding AI-generated content. The Commission evaluates measures taken by Member States concerning AI practices to ensure alignment with EU law, promoting the standardization of activities linked to quality management.

Additionally, the Commission oversees compliance with both national and EU regulations pertaining to AI, including the management of an EU database for high-risk AI systems. It identifies general-purpose AI models that may present systemic risks, engages with stakeholders to establish performance metrics and benchmarks, and assesses certification and compliance costs for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Furthermore, it serves as the main point of contact for reporting serious incidents involving AI models, fostering a responsible AI ecosystem.

Operating under the framework of Regulation (EU) No 182/2011, the Commission enhances its decision-making capabilities and oversees penalties that Member States may impose during AI-related litigation. It also facilitates access to experts for Member States and encourages the adoption of voluntary codes of conduct related to AI systems. These efforts underline the Commission's commitment to effective governance and regulation in the evolving landscapes of AI and biometric identification systems within the EU, while also promoting AI literacy among relevant stakeholders.<SEP>The Commission refers to the European Commission, responsible for establishing data spaces and facilitating data sharing among businesses and government entities.

Regulation (EU) No 182/2011
Regulation (EU) No 182/2011 outlines procedural rules for the EU's legislative decision-making process and serves as a legal reference in the context mentioned.<SEP>Regulation (EU) No 182/2011 outlines the rules and principles for the control exercised by Member States over the EU Commission's implementing powers.

Committee
The Committee is a group that assists the Commission and operates under the regulations specified in Regulation (EU) No 182/2011.

European Parliament
The European Parliament is a crucial legislative body within the European Union (EU) that plays a significant role in the creation, amendment, and enactment of laws affecting member states across various sectors. It is directly elected to represent the interests of EU citizens and is engaged in discussions and decisions related to a broad range of policies, including technology, cybersecurity, migration, asylum, labor regulations, consumer protection, and commercial practices.

In its legislative capacity, the European Parliament collaborates closely with the Council of the EU and the European Commission to develop and oversee regulations and directives. Its actions are reflective of the concerns and needs of EU citizens, with a strong emphasis on ethical considerations in emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence (AI). This commitment is evidenced by initiatives like the Directive (EU) 2022/2557, which addresses high-risk AI systems, as well as the significant Digital Services Act and Directive (EU) 2019/1937.

The European Parliament is responsible for proposing and approving legislation, ensuring compliance and transparency within the EU legal framework. It actively receives reports and assessments from the Commission concerning the enforcement of AI-related regulations and establishes rules governing various aspects of life in the EU, which include technology, safety, copyright, digital markets, and the regulation of medical devices and machinery.

Overall, the European Parliament's responsibilities encompass not only legislative decision-making but also budgeting and the development of directives and regulations that adequately address the complexities and needs of the EU populace. This makes it an integral part of the EU's legislative structure, representing the citizens of member states and ensuring their voices are heard in the legislative process.<SEP>The European Parliament is one of the legislative bodies of the European Union, involved in the creation and amendment of regulations like 2018/858 and 2024/1689.

Directive (EU) 2020/1828
Directive (EU) 2020/1828 focuses on improving the safety of consumer products and is relevant to AI systems regulation.<SEP>Directive (EU) 2020/1828 is legislation concerning collective actions for consumer protection, repealing previous directives.<SEP>Directive (EU) 2020/1828 pertains to consumer protection laws in the digital context, also relevant to AI regulation.<SEP>Directive (EU) 2020/1828 relates to collective actions for the protection of consumers, ensuring their interests are upheld in the digital marketplace.<SEP>Directive (EU) 2020/1828 relates to the improvement of the protection of collective interests of consumers, particularly in terms of sustainable consumption.

Regulation (EU) 2024/1689
Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 establishes harmonized rules concerning artificial intelligence systems as safety components within the EU.<SEP>Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 is a comprehensive legislative act established by the European Parliament and Council, aimed at creating harmonized rules for artificial intelligence (AI) within the European Union. This regulation not only lays down standardized provisions for AI systems but also amends several existing regulations to ensure compliance and enhance safety in the deployment of AI technologies. As an upcoming legal framework, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 focuses on ensuring that AI systems adhere to stipulated safety standards and operational guidelines, thereby promoting a structured and secure integration of artificial intelligence across the EU.<SEP>Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 is a legislative act by the European Parliament that outlines harmonized rules on artificial intelligence systems.<SEP>Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 is a legal framework that lays down harmonized rules on artificial intelligence, impacting safety components in various sectors.<SEP>Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 is a legislative act by the European Parliament setting harmonized rules on artificial intelligence and amending several previous regulations and directives.

Artificial Intelligence Act
The Artificial Intelligence Act includes comprehensive regulations that outline legal frameworks for the development and implementation of AI systems in the EU.<SEP>The Artificial Intelligence Act is a regulatory proposal by the European Union that aims to establish a comprehensive legal framework for the use and governance of artificial intelligence technologies within its member states. Officially known as Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Act seeks to promote innovation while ensuring safety, ethical standards, and compliance across various sectors. It includes detailed provisions that outline safety requirements and compliance measures for AI systems, thereby providing harmonized rules to manage the development and application of artificial intelligence throughout the EU. Through this legislation, the EU intends to govern the use and development of AI, ensuring that all AI systems adhere to established safety and ethical guidelines.

European Parliament and Council
The European Parliament and Council collaboratively enact regulations and directives for the governance of the European Union.<SEP>The European Parliament and Council together represent the legislative power of the European Union, playing a significant role in creating laws and regulations.

Regulations (EC) No 300/2008
Regulation (EC) No 300/2008 outlines security provisions for the civil aviation industry, contributing to broader safety regulations for transport.<SEP>Regulations (EC) No 300/2008 relates to security operational standards for civil aviation in the EU.

Regulations (EU) No 167/2013
Regulations (EU) No 167/2013 focus on the type-approval of agricultural and forestry vehicles in the EU.<SEP>Regulations (EU) No 167/2013 governs the approval and market surveillance of agricultural and forestry vehicles in the European Union.

Regulations (EU) No 168/2013
Regulations (EU) No 168/2013 pertains to the approval and market surveillance of two or three wheeled vehicles in the European Union.<SEP>Regulations (EU) No 168/2013 set safety rules for the type-approval of two- or three-wheeled vehicles and quadricycles in the EU.

Regulations (EU) 2018/858
Regulation (EU) 2018/858 relates to the approval and market surveillance of motor vehicles and their trailers, ensuring compliance with safety and environmental standards.<SEP>Regulations (EU) 2018/858 outlines the approval and market surveillance of motor vehicles within the European Union.

Regulations (EU) 2018/1139
Regulations (EU) 2018/1139 establish rules for civil aviation safety and the operations of the European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA).<SEP>Regulations (EU) 2018/1139 focuses on the safety of civil aviation operations and the regulation of commercial air transport.

Regulations (EU) 2019/2144
Regulations (EU) 2019/2144 establishes the framework for the approval of motor vehicles with respect to their environmental performance.<SEP>Regulations (EU) 2019/2144 set requirements for the approval of motor vehicles regarding cybersecurity and software updates.

OJ L 409
OJ L 409 refers to a specific event or publication, dated 4.12.2020, likely associated with legal documentation or legislative matters.

4.12.2020
The date 4.12.2020 marks when OJ L 409 was published, indicating its relevance in a specific timeframe.

publication
Publication refers to the act of making information available to the public, often involving legal or regulatory content.

Official Journal of the European Union
The Official Journal of the European Union is the official publication of the European Union, serving as a vital source for disseminating legal documents, announcements, and legislative acts. It plays a crucial role in publishing information related to EU regulations and compliance standards, including aspects related to cybersecurity requirements. Additionally, the journal provides references to harmonized standards, which are essential for compliance assessments. Overall, the Official Journal of the European Union is the primary platform for the official publication and dissemination of EU legislation and regulatory information.<SEP>The Official Journal of the European Union is the publication in which EU legislation and decisions are officially published.<SEP>The Official Journal of the European Union is the publication through which the EU publishes its legislative acts and notifications.

legal documentation
Legal documentation includes official texts, regulations, and announcements which are published to inform the public and relevant stakeholders.

AI Regulatory Sandbox
The AI Regulatory Sandbox refers to controlled environments established by competent authorities to facilitate the development, testing, and training of innovative and high-risk AI systems. This framework is designed to enable stakeholders, including small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and start-ups, to experiment with AI technologies while adhering to strict regulatory requirements and safeguards that ensure compliance with national and Union laws. 

The primary goal of the AI Regulatory Sandbox is to promote the safe and effective implementation of AI technologies by providing a structured regulatory environment where developers can test their AI products under specific eligibility criteria. This environment allows for the use of personal data in developing AI systems under specific legal conditions, ensuring that public interest is protected across various sectors. Overall, the AI Regulatory Sandbox serves as a vital tool for advancing innovation in AI while maintaining regulatory oversight and compliance.<SEP>The AI regulatory sandbox is a controlled testing environment for AI systems to ensure compliance with regulations while enabling innovation.

Public Safety
Public safety encompasses various measures aimed at protecting individuals and communities, especially concerning health care systems and emergency responses.

Public Health
Public health involves efforts to prevent disease and promote health through organized community efforts and public policies.

Climate Change Mitigation
Climate change mitigation applies AI to model climate impacts, improve resource management, and support adaptive strategies.<SEP>Climate change mitigation consists of actions aimed at reducing the severity of climate change effects through environmental protection measures.

Energy Sustainability
Energy sustainability refers to the endeavor to provide energy in a way that meets current needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet their own needs.

Transport Systems
Transport systems encompass the infrastructure and operations involved in moving people and goods efficiently and safely.

Public Administration
Public administration includes the implementation of government policies and the management of public programs and services.

Data Processing
Data processing refers to the handling and manipulation of collected data for specific purposes, such as development and testing of AI systems.

Public Authority
A public authority is a government agency or body that exercises regulatory authority and provides public services.<SEP>Public authorities are organizations or government entities responsible for protecting public interest and implementing laws, often playing a role in AI development.

Natural or Legal Person
A Natural or Legal Person can be an individual or organization that has legal rights and responsibilities, especially in relation to overseeing published content.<SEP>A natural or legal person is any individual or legal entity with grounds to submit complaints regarding possible infringements of regulations.<SEP>A natural or legal person refers to an individual or an entity (like a corporation) that can enter into legal agreements and has rights and responsibilities.<SEP>A natural or legal person refers to any individual or legal entity that has legal rights and obligations, relevant in the context of confidentiality and data protection.

Union Data Protection Law
Union data protection law consists of legal frameworks that govern the protection of personal data within the European Union.<SEP>Union data protection law provides legal frameworks for the handling of personal data within the EU, ensuring users' rights are protected.<SEP>Union data protection laws are regulations put in place to protect personal data and safeguard individuals' rights concerning their data.

Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679
Article 35 outlines the requirements for conducting Data Protection Impact Assessments in the context of personal data processing.

Article 39 of Regulation (EU) 2018/1725
Article 39 pertains to the evaluation and supervision of personal data processing activities in specific areas.

Monitoring Mechanisms
Monitoring mechanisms ensure compliance with regulations and assess risks to individuals involved in data processing activities.

Response Mechanisms
Response mechanisms involve procedures established to mitigate any risks to rights and freedoms of data subjects during data processing.

Regulation (EU) 2018/1725
Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 focuses on the processing of personal data by Union institutions and bodies, ensuring similar protections as those in the GDPR.<SEP>Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 focuses on the protection of personal data by EU institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies, ensuring compliance with data protection standards.<SEP>Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 is a comprehensive legal framework established to ensure the protection of personal data within European Union (EU) institutions and bodies. It outlines specific provisions related to the processing of personal data, emphasizing the safeguarding of individuals' rights and privacy. This regulation applies to various EU entities, including institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies, and governs the use and management of data and databases, notably including the EU database for artificial intelligence (AI) systems.

In addition to addressing general data protection, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 includes provisions relevant to the processing of personal data within AI regulatory sandboxes. It encompasses rules surrounding the handling of various types of data, including sensitive biometric data, thereby ensuring compliance with data protection standards across the EU.

Overall, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 is crucial for ensuring that personal data processing by EU institutions is conducted in a manner that respects and protects the privacy rights of individuals.

Sandbox Experimentation
Sandbox experimentation refers to controlled environments where innovative AI systems can be tested with personal data under specific regulatory conditions.

Competent Authorities
Competent Authorities are designated regulatory bodies with a multifaceted role in overseeing the compliance and safety standards associated with various regulatory frameworks, particularly in relation to biometric data processing and artificial intelligence (AI). Their primary responsibility is to enforce laws and regulations pertaining to biometric data processing, which includes ensuring compliance with data protection legislation. 

In the realm of AI, Competent Authorities are tasked with supervising the deployment and operation of high-risk AI systems. They hold specific supervisory powers that enable them to oversee testing, monitoring, and adherence to regulatory frameworks at both Union and national levels. These authorities work in close collaboration with the AI Office to ensure compliance with various AI regulations, reflecting their integral role in the governance of AI technologies. This includes managing the implementation of AI projects and enhancing transparency by publishing relevant information on their respective websites.

Competent Authorities play a critical role in ensuring that high-risk AI systems meet appropriate safety and legal standards. They are also responsible for reporting and investigating serious incidents related to AI, which underscores their importance in maintaining accountability and upholding safety standards within the AI landscape. Furthermore, they oversee the application and enforcement of financial regulations, particularly those impacting AI in financial services, guiding entities involved in data processing to navigate compliance requirements appropriately.

Overall, Competent Authorities operate as the cornerstone of regulatory oversight, enforcing compliance and guiding the development and testing of AI systems while ensuring that associated risks are managed effectively.<SEP>Competent Authorities are governmental bodies responsible for overseeing the implementation of regulations and ensuring compliance among market operators.<SEP>Competent Authorities are regulatory bodies tasked with overseeing the implementation and management of AI regulatory sandboxes, ensuring compliance with laws and regulations during the development of AI systems.<SEP>Competent Authorities are regulatory bodies responsible for overseeing the implementation of the regulation and ensuring access to high-quality data for AI training and validation.

Law Enforcement Authorities
Law Enforcement Authorities are governmental bodies tasked with maintaining public order and ensuring public safety. Their primary responsibilities include preventing, investigating, detecting, and prosecuting criminal offenses, which are essential for overall public security. These authorities operate within legal frameworks that govern the processing of personal data, ensuring compliance while performing their duties related to public safety and criminal justice.

As part of their efforts to combat crime, Law Enforcement Authorities often integrate advanced technologies, particularly artificial intelligence (AI) systems. These technologies assist in assessing risks and conducting investigations into criminal activities. They also engage in identity verification and conduct identity checks as part of their law enforcement responsibilities. The deployment of high-risk AI systems, particularly for biometric identification, occurs under specific legal regulations, highlighting the balance between technological advancement and compliance with protective data provisions.

Law Enforcement Authorities encompass a range of organizations responsible for enforcing laws, maintaining public order, and safeguarding national security. While they may utilize high-risk AI systems under certain circumstances, they do so under strict legal frameworks, ensuring both the effectiveness of their operations and the protection of individual rights. Overall, Law Enforcement Authorities play a crucial role in crime prevention and prosecution while adapting to the evolving landscape of technology and law enforcement practices.<SEP>Law Enforcement Authorities utilize AI systems and have specific conformity assessment procedures stipulated in the regulations.<SEP>Law enforcement authorities are governmental organizations responsible for maintaining public order and enforcing the law, and they play a critical role in the deployment of biometric identification systems.<SEP>Law enforcement authorities are government agencies responsible for maintaining public order and enforcing laws, with specific considerations during the monitoring of AI systems.

Article 39
Article 39 refers to a specific provision within Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 that discusses the requirements and procedures related to sandbox experimentation.

Sandbox
A sandbox is a controlled environment that allows experimentation and testing of AI systems under specific regulations and supervision.<SEP>The sandbox is a controlled testing environment designed for innovative technologies, particularly AI systems, allowing for experimentation with personal data under regulatory oversight.

Personal Data
Personal Data is defined as any information that relates to an identified or identifiable individual. This type of data plays a significant role in the context of artificial intelligence systems and is governed by a range of regulations, notably the Regulation (EU) 2016/679. Personal Data encompasses all information processed by organizations concerning an identifiable natural person, ensuring that such data is subject to protection under various data protection laws, particularly those enacted in the European Union. 

This category of data also includes special types of information that require careful handling due to their sensitive nature. The handling of Personal Data must adhere to strict data protection regulations to maintain privacy and compliance within existing regulatory frameworks. Overall, Personal Data is crucial for safeguarding individual privacy rights while being involved in the deployment and utilization of AI components for diverse purposes.<SEP>Personal data encompasses any information that can identify an individual, such as names, addresses, and other identifiers, and must be handled according to data protection laws.<SEP>Personal data refers to any information relating to individuals that must be protected and deleted after testing.<SEP>Personal data refers to any data that relates to an identified or identifiable individual, which is protected under various regulations including GDPR.

Technical Documentation
Documentation prepared by AI model providers detailing the usage and capabilities of their models for compliance and transparency.<SEP>Technical Documentation is a comprehensive collection of essential records and documents necessary to demonstrate compliance with regulatory standards for high-risk AI systems. This documentation serves multiple purposes and is crucial prior to the marketing or use of these AI systems. It encompasses detailed information regarding the development, testing, and validation processes of the AI system, along with associated test results and project summaries.

Furthermore, Technical Documentation includes records that articulate the rationale and outcomes of AI experiments conducted within controlled environments, often referred to as sandboxes. It ensures that all necessary information required to verify compliance and operational performance is meticulously maintained by providers. The documentation must adhere to the regulatory framework outlined in Annex XI, which assures that all necessary standards are met for the safe and effective deployment of AI technologies.

In addition to showcasing the compliance related to the deployment of these systems, Technical Documentation outlines the post-market monitoring and compliance processes. It represents the necessary paperwork that provides insights into the compliance and functioning of high-risk AI systems, encompassing detailed descriptions and instructions that must be retained by providers for regulatory adherence.<SEP>Technical documentation encompasses detailed records and descriptions of AI model functionalities, modifications, and data sources necessary for compliance.<SEP>Technical Documentation is necessary for High-Risk AI Systems as it outlines the design, function, and operational processes relevant to the AI application.

Union Law
Union Law encompasses all legal regulations and directives applicable within the governance framework of the European Union.<SEP>Union Law represents a comprehensive legal framework established by the European Union (EU) that governs a wide array of regulatory practices across various sectors, with a particular emphasis on biometric data and artificial intelligence (AI) systems. This body of legislation is designed to delineate the liability and responsibilities of providers during the testing and implementation of these technologies, ultimately aiming to safeguard public interests and uphold fundamental rights within the EU.

Within its scope, Union Law outlines acceptable practices and classification standards for the use of biometric data, ensuring a responsible approach to digital services while drawing attention to their societal impacts. It focuses on enhancing risk management procedures for AI systems, especially in sensitive areas such as law enforcement, where it seeks to mitigate risks linked to discrimination and the infringement of individual rights.

Additionally, Union Law encompasses broad data protection regulations that govern the lawful use of personal information and addresses the evaluation practices of individuals. Important provisions are included to protect the rights of copyright holders regarding permissible data use for AI training, promoting fair usage of information and addressing the challenges associated with personal data processing in AI applications.

Central to Union Law are the principles of equality and non-discrimination, which underpin the structured oversight mechanisms designed to prevent discrimination in the deployment of AI systems through adherence to compliance standards. Moreover, it comprises regulations applicable at the union level that impact multiple sectors, including high-risk technologies, migration, border control, and workplace rights.

Overall, Union Law is a crucial framework that intricately regulates the interaction between AI technology, data protection, and individual rights within the EU. It embodies a significant legislative effort to navigate the complexities of modern technology while upholding the values of the Union and ensuring compliance across its member states.

Data Subjects
Data subjects are individuals whose personal data is being processed, and they hold rights under data protection laws including consent for data usage.<SEP>Data subjects are individuals whose personal data is being processed, having specific rights and protections under data protection laws.

AI Project
The AI Project developed in the sandbox aims to execute specific objectives and expected results, while being documented and summarized by competent authorities.

AI System
AI Systems refer to a category of advanced technologies that utilize artificial intelligence to perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence, such as understanding natural language, recognizing patterns, making decisions, and generating and editing content. These systems are versatile and find applications across various sectors, including civilian, humanitarian, and military contexts. They consist of diverse components, including models, tools, and processes that enable them to exhibit intelligent behavior.

In the context of the European Union, AI Systems are classified as high-risk technologies due to their significant potential implications for health, safety, and fundamental rights. This classification necessitates strict compliance with specific regulations governing their deployment and usage. High-risk AI Systems undergo rigorous evaluations by notified bodies to ensure they meet market regulations. This process is supported by regulatory frameworks such as AI regulatory sandboxes, which facilitate the training, testing, and validation of these systems in real-world scenarios while emphasizing risk management.

Providers of AI Systems bear the responsibility for designing and determining the intended functionalities of these systems, ensuring they are deployed responsibly and safely across various domains. Despite their engineering aimed at enhancing human activities and outcomes, concerns regarding data protection rights are raised by their operations. Therefore, adherence to oversight and conformity assessments based on legislative regulations is crucial for effectively managing associated risks.

Furthermore, AI Systems require specific mechanisms for their proper functioning and maintenance, including routine software updates and logging procedures. They are designed to operate autonomously but have established protocols for their recall during testing phases under real-world conditions. Overall, AI Systems represent significant technological advancements with a wide range of applications, demanding careful consideration and compliance with legal and ethical standards to mitigate potential risks and uphold fundamental rights.<SEP>AI systems refer to artificial intelligence technologies that are subject to testing and regulation as per the guidelines set by market surveillance authorities.

Annex IV
Annex IV is a critical component of regulatory frameworks concerning high-risk AI systems, containing specific technical documentation guidelines that impact the evaluation and assessment of modifications made to those systems. It outlines the requirements for technical documentation related to the conformity assessment process, ensuring that any substantial modifications are adequately reported and evaluated. Furthermore, Annex IV refers to a section within regulations that details necessary elements for the technical documentation of high-risk AI systems, including guidance on AI monitoring plans. It is designed to ensure compliance with required information and technical standards, which may be amended by the Commission as necessary, thereby providing a structured approach to managing the complexities of AI projects and their modifications.

Union Law on Personal Data
Union Law on Personal Data sets the legal standards for processing personal data, ensuring compliance in the context of AI systems and other innovations.

Criminal Offences
Criminal Offences are violations against the law that law enforcement authorities are tasked with preventing, investigating, and prosecuting.<SEP>Criminal Offences encompass acts that are punishable by law, requiring enforcement and prosecution by designated authorities.<SEP>Criminal offences encompass a range of illegal activities that law enforcement authorities aim to prevent, investigate, and prosecute.<SEP>Criminal Offences refer to specific violations of law that are outlined in the Union's legal framework, including those potentially linked to biometric identification.<SEP>Criminal offences are actions or omissions that violate the law and are subject to prosecution.

Public Security
Public Security pertains to the measures taken to ensure the safety and protection of citizens, often involving law enforcement activities.<SEP>Public security involves measures taken to ensure the safety and order of the public, often facilitated by law enforcement agencies.<SEP>Public Security refers to the protection of citizens from threats and emergencies, often influencing when and how AI systems are deployed.<SEP>Public security refers to the safety and protection of citizens and assets, which may necessitate the use of AI technology under urgent conditions.

AI
AI (Artificial Intelligence) is a rapidly evolving family of technologies that impact various industries by enhancing prediction, optimising operations, and personalising digital solutions.<SEP>Artificial Intelligence (AI) is a rapidly developing family of technologies encompassing various applications and systems that require careful regulation and oversight. Defined as a field of study within computer science, AI focuses on creating systems capable of performing tasks typically requiring human intelligence, such as learning and problem-solving. While AI possesses significant potential for beneficial uses, it also carries inherent risks, including the possibility of misuse in manipulative and exploitative practices. To address these concerns, new regulations are being established to ensure the safety, protection of fundamental rights, and proper functioning of AI in the market. AI systems can pose risks and cause harm to public interests and rights when applied carelessly in different contexts.<SEP>AI refers to artificial intelligence technologies that are designed to perform tasks that would typically require human intelligence, such as reasoning, learning, and problem-solving.<SEP>AI refers to artificial intelligence, a significant technological development that can greatly impact society and should adhere to ethical and regulatory standards.<SEP>AI refers to artificial intelligence, which involves the simulation of human intelligence processes by machines, especially computer systems.

Union
The Union refers to the European Union (EU), a political and economic alliance comprising a collective of member states primarily located in Europe. This entity operates under a framework of agreed treaties and regulations, emphasizing cooperation among its member nations to establish common policies and guidelines, particularly concerning the deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) systems. 

At the core of the Union’s mission is the establishment of a robust regulatory framework aimed at promoting trustworthy AI. This includes developing standards that govern the creation, use, and regulation of AI technologies, particularly focusing on effectively managing and enforcing regulations concerning high-risk AI systems. The Union actively collaborates with competent authorities from its member states to ensure compliance and foster innovation, especially among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). To facilitate this, initiatives like regulatory sandboxes are implemented to enable experimental projects within a controlled regulatory environment.

In addition to its focus on AI governance, the Union places significant emphasis on data privacy and the protection of personal information, enhancing its regulatory landscape in these areas. It oversees compliance related to AI models and their providers, upholding the collective interests of its member nations. The Union also regulates various laws concerning data protection, nondiscrimination, consumer protection, and competition law, thereby reinforcing standardized regulatory approaches to support technological development and shared economic goals.

Moreover, the Union encompasses broader cooperation among European countries on a range of policies, including law enforcement, migration, border control, and asylum. It acts as an organized body that provides legal frameworks and protections for individuals and corporations regarding their rights and freedoms. Overall, the Union functions as a comprehensive entity dedicated to advancing technological development while maintaining governance and compliance to benefit its member states collectively.

Charter
The Charter is a foundational document within the European Union that embodies and enshrines a set of fundamental rights, including health, safety, democracy, the rule of law, nondiscrimination, data protection, privacy, and the rights of the child. It serves as a guiding document that reflects the core values and principles that the Union upholds. The Charter guarantees various rights such as freedom of expression and the arts, which are particularly relevant when considering the implications of AI technologies in creative works. Its provisions primarily impact the deployment of AI systems and the legal principles surrounding personal data processing, emphasizing the importance of protecting individual rights in the context of technological advancement. Overall, the Charter plays a crucial role in shaping the legal and ethical framework of the European Union, ensuring that fundamental rights are respected and upheld.<SEP>The Charter serves as a basis for establishing common rules and standards for various rights, including health and safety.<SEP>The Charter outlines fundamental rights and freedoms, ensuring protection for various human rights including dignity, privacy, and non-discrimination.<SEP>The Charter refers to the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, which explains the fundamental rights and freedoms protected within the EU framework.

Human Dignity
Human dignity is a foundational principle in the development of AI, emphasizing the respect for individuals' rights and personal integrity.<SEP>Human dignity is a fundamental value that emphasizes the inherent worth of every individual and is a core principle safeguarded by the Union.

Freedom
Freedom refers to the state of being free from oppressive restrictions imposed by authority on one's way of life, behavior, or political views, an important value upheld by the Union.

Equality
Equality signifies the state of being equal, especially in status, rights, and opportunities, and is a fundamental principle promoted by the Union.

Democracy
Democracy is a system of government by the whole population, typically through elected representatives, representing another key value of the Union.<SEP>Democracy is a system of government in which power is vested in the people, who rule either directly or through freely elected representatives.

Rule of Law
The rule of law is the principle that all people and institutions are subject to and accountable to the law, ensuring fairness in legal matters, which the Union supports.

AI Systems
AI Systems are sophisticated technological frameworks that harness artificial intelligence to execute tasks typically requiring human intelligence, such as decision-making, problem-solving, and behavior prediction based on data inputs. These systems incorporate a variety of AI technologies and methodologies, and they are classified by associated risk levels, particularly concerning health, safety, and fundamental rights. High-risk AI Systems, which may involve biometric identification and extensive data analysis to predict behaviors, are subjected to rigorous regulatory measures owing to their significant implications for individual rights and societal welfare. This has sparked essential discussions about transparency and the ethical use of these technologies.

The integration of AI Systems is widespread, spanning diverse sectors such as military operations, security, law enforcement, humanitarian efforts, and national security. They enhance responses to criminal activities through effective risk assessment and evidence evaluation. By combining general-purpose AI models with user interfaces, AI Systems improve operational efficiency and decision-making processes. Continuous research, performance evaluations, and regulatory oversight are vital to maintaining accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity throughout their existence.

In addition to their operational roles, AI Systems significantly affect human behavior in key areas, including electoral processes and workplace decision-making. These systems utilize algorithms and analytics for applications such as facial recognition, which raises important privacy concerns. In workplace contexts, AI Systems are crucial for recruitment, evaluation, and management decisions, highlighting the necessity of addressing their ethical implications upon deployment.

AI Systems are also employed to evaluate or score individuals based on social behavior, personal characteristics, and contextual information. In specialized fields like migration, asylum, and border control management, these technologies aim to enhance operational efficiency while adhering to legal frameworks, underscoring the need for governance and ethical compliance to mitigate associated risks.

Recognized as high-risk products, AI Systems require adherence to established regulations to manage risks and ensure safety, particularly within the European Union context. Their transformative potential emphasizes the necessity for ethical governance and responsible deployment, prioritizing standards that effectively address inherent risks while promoting beneficial societal integration. Furthermore, robust cybersecurity measures are crucial to safeguard against threats and vulnerabilities linked to these systems, which can include manipulative designs that may distort human behavior based on their functionality and application. Finally, AI Systems are also utilized in the education sector to improve digital education and training, focusing on vital skills such as media literacy and critical thinking.<SEP>AI Systems refer to software and algorithms that perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence, including learning, reasoning, and problem-solving.<SEP>AI systems refer to technologies designed to identify individuals remotely through biometric data in public spaces, often used for law enforcement purposes.<SEP>AI systems are technologies designed to interact with natural persons, generating content and performing tasks, raising issues of impersonation and deception.<SEP>AI Systems refer to software and technologies that perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence, which are subject to regulations requiring enforcement.

Public and Private Entities
Public and private entities are organizations that may develop or utilize AI systems for various purposes, including military and defense.

Member States
Member States are countries that are part of the European Union (EU), serving as individual sovereign entities that comprise the larger political and economic union. They play a critical role in the EU's collective governance and regulatory framework, actively participating in the application and enforcement of EU laws and regulations across various sectors, including immigration, human rights, artificial intelligence (AI), medical devices, and law enforcement. 

As integral components of the EU's governance structure, Member States are bound by its treaties and regulations, ensuring compliance with directives through collaboration. They designate representatives to a Board responsible for overseeing discussions on AI regulations, contributing to the implementation and enforcement of AI policies. This cooperative governance allows Member States to engage in dialogues that balance innovation with the protection of workers’ rights and national security.

To support responsible innovation, Member States have established regulatory sandboxes to manage potential risks associated with new technologies. Conformity Assessment Procedure is the process of verifying that AI systems comply with relevant regulations and standards prior to deployment.<SEP>The Conformity Assessment Procedure is a defined guideline under the regulation that stipulates how products must be evaluated for compliance with cybersecurity standards.<SEP>The Conformity Assessment Procedure is a formal and systematic process designed to evaluate whether high-risk AI systems comply with established safety standards and regulatory requirements. Annex III
Annex III is a crucial component of regulatory documents pertaining to artificial intelligence (AI) systems within the European Union (EU). It encompasses a classification of high-risk AI systems that are subject to specific regulations and oversight, particularly due to their potential impact on safety and fundamental rights. The annex provides a comprehensive framework for regulatory oversight, detailing the criteria for classifying various types of high-risk AI systems, including those utilized by financial institutions that necessitate enhanced scrutiny.

The descriptions highlight that Annex III includes a list of specific AI systems that require regulation, emphasizing the serious risks these high-risk systems pose to multiple Member States. It aims to ensure a harmonized approach to regulation across the EU by outlining detailed standards for risk evaluation. Furthermore, the annex delineates the regulatory requirements embedded in the legal frameworks and specifies the conditions that determine whether an AI system is categorized as high-risk.

Annex III is closely associated with Regulation (EU) 2019/1020, which addresses the necessary protocols and standards for high-risk AI systems, necessitating careful evaluation and oversight to safeguard public interests. Overall, Annex III plays an essential role in establishing regulatory obligations and conformity assessment procedures for the deployment of high-risk AI systems within the regulatory framework.<SEP>Annex III outlines the provisions and requirements for high-risk AI systems in relation to testing and regulation.<SEP>Annex III refers to a specific section of regulations that outlines the requirements for testing high-risk AI systems in various areas, including law enforcement and migration.<SEP>Annex III outlines the specific AI systems that have a maximum certificate validity period of four years.

Article 97
Article 97 is a significant provision within the regulatory framework that grants the Commission the authority to adopt delegated acts aimed at modifying regulations concerning artificial intelligence (AI) systems and their associated risks. This article specifically empowers the Commission to amend technical documentation to ensure compliance with established requirements. Furthermore, it outlines the provisions under which the Commission can adjust regulations related to high-risk categories of AI systems, including the ability to modify the list of high-risk AI systems as needed.

In addition to these powers, Article 97 delineates the responsibilities of the Commission in relation to regulatory compliance, authorizing it to elaborate on methodologies and amend annexes in response to advancements in technology. Overall, Article 97 serves as a crucial mechanism for maintaining up-to-date regulations that reflect the evolving landscape of AI technology and its associated risks.<SEP>Article 97 outlines the procedures and powers granted to The Commission for amending legislative acts.<SEP>Article 97 refers to a legal provision that guides the Commission in adopting delegated acts concerning AI model classifications and thresholds.

Use-cases of High-Risk AI Systems

National Competent Authorities
National Competent Authorities (NCAs) are designated governmental bodies within the European Union responsible for overseeing and ensuring compliance of artificial intelligence (AI) systems with relevant regulations in their respective jurisdictions. They play a crucial role in monitoring high-risk AI systems to ensure adherence to legal and safety standards, thereby safeguarding fundamental rights throughout the deployment and operation of these technologies.

The primary functions of NCAs include assessing and enforcing regulations, supervising the implementation of AI regulatory sandboxes, and providing essential support for compliance with laws. They are tasked with reporting any adverse effects of AI systems to the relevant European Commission, contributing to a transparent and accountable AI ecosystem. Composed of experts in AI technologies, data protection, cybersecurity, and legal standards, NCAs operate independently and impartially, ensuring objectivity in their regulatory functions.

In addition to their monitoring responsibilities, NCAs facilitate the operation of AI regulatory sandboxes at the national level, designed to evaluate AI systems' implementation and to confirm their regulatory compliance. They inform applicants of their compliance-related decisions, maintaining the integrity of the AI sector. NCAs hold the authority to manage legal infringements and may impose administrative fines according to the national legal framework.

Overall, National Competent Authorities are essential for the safe and responsible adoption of AI technologies, reaffirming their commitment to safety, legal compliance, and fundamental rights. They function as local regulatory entities focused on fostering a compliant AI landscape within their jurisdictions, ensuring that providers of high-risk AI systems adhere to relevant regulations and standards.<SEP>Official organizations responsible for overseeing the implementation of regulations related to AI models and monitoring compliance among providers.<SEP>National Competent Authorities are entities responsible for establishing and managing AI regulatory sandboxes in their jurisdictions, ensuring compliance and cooperation with other regulatory bodies.<SEP>National Competent Authorities are organizations responsible for overseeing the implementation of regulations and ensuring compliance within their jurisdictions, especially regarding AI systems.

Technical Solutions
Technical Solutions are the methods and technologies available to correct or mitigate adverse impacts caused by AI systems, focusing on health, safety, and rights.<SEP>Technical Solutions refer to methodologies or technologies available to correct or reverse harmful outcomes produced by AI systems.<SEP>Technical solutions are methods required for marking and detecting AI-generated content to differentiate it from human-generated content.<SEP>Technical solutions refer to methods and tools used to ensure AI systems are effective, reliable, and comply with standards.<SEP>Technical solutions encompass the tools and methods used to facilitate the development and implementation of AI technologies in an ethical and efficient manner.

Harm

Adverse Impact
Adverse Impact represents the unintended negative consequences that may arise from AI system outputs, particularly on vulnerable populations.

Dependence on AI Outcomes

Delegated Acts
Delegated Acts are legal instruments that allow the Commission to amend regulations, including criteria regarding systemic risks associated with AI models.<SEP>Delegated Acts are regulatory measures that the Commission can adopt to amend existing laws regarding high-risk AI systems based on evolving understandings or assessments of risk.<SEP>Delegated Acts denote the legal provisions enabling the Commission to implement amendments and updates to existing regulations related to AI.<SEP>Delegated acts are legal acts of the EU that enable the European Commission to supplement or amend non-essential parts of legally binding Union acts.<SEP>Delegated acts are powers granted to the Commission to amend specific annexes and regulations relating to AI compliance as technology evolves.

The Commission
The Commission is a governing body within the European Union, vested with multiple responsibilities related to the regulation and implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Acting as the executive branch of the EU, the Commission plays a crucial role in developing guidelines and regulatory frameworks related to AI, including the establishment of an AI regulatory sandbox. Its functions encompass proposing legislation, enforcing laws, and managing various administrative tasks aimed at ensuring compliant AI practices.

In addition to its legislative responsibilities, the Commission actively engages in consultations with Member States to address any objections concerning assessments and authorizations related to AI technologies. The Commission oversees the designation of Union AI Testing Support Structures and is tasked with adopting guidelines and delegated acts pertinent to AI regulations, ensuring that safety standards are maintained within the AI landscape.

Furthermore, the Commission is responsible for coordinating and ensuring cooperation among notified bodies concerning high-risk AI systems and compliance procedures. As an authoritative body with exclusive powers, it supervises and enforces specific regulations under the Treaties, safeguarding various interests, including public security and confidentiality. Through its efforts, the Commission aims to enhance the governance surrounding AI, aligning it with EU policies and promoting responsible innovation in this evolving field.<SEP>The Commission refers to the European Commission, which is in charge of issuing requests for standardisation and ensuring regulatory compliance in various sectors including AI.<SEP>The Commission refers to an authoritative body that can impose fines on providers of general-purpose AI models for regulatory non-compliance.<SEP>The Commission is an entity that may develop initiatives to facilitate the lowering of technical barriers for AI development and promote cross-border data exchange.<SEP>The Commission is responsible for investigating the competence of notified bodies and ensuring compliance with regulatory requirements.

Autonomous Robots
Autonomous robots are increasingly capable machines designed for various roles in manufacturing, personal assistance, and care, requiring safety in operation.

Health Sector
The Health Sector includes all services and entities involved in the delivery of healthcare and medical data, emphasizing the importance of AI in improving health outcomes.<SEP>The health sector encompasses organizations and systems involved in medical care and health services where the stakes for life and health are critical.

Diagnostics Systems

Manufacturing
Manufacturing involves the production of goods and requires adherence to safety standards when employing advanced technologies like AI and robotics.

Personal Assistance

Care

Digital Components

Post-Remote Biometric Identification Systems
Post-Remote Biometric Identification Systems are AI technologies utilized by law enforcement to identify individuals based on biometric data, subject to strict regulatory oversight.<SEP>Post-remote biometric identification systems refer to technologies used to identify individuals from video footage after the fact and have specific privacy regulations associated with their use.

Surveillance
Surveillance involves monitoring individuals or groups, often through technologies, to gather information, typically for security or law enforcement purposes.

Data Protection
Data protection refers to the process of safeguarding personal data from misuse or unauthorized access, as mandated by various regulations and laws.

Notified Bodies
Notified Bodies are accredited organizations established under national law in EU Member States, playing a vital role in assessing the conformity of high-risk AI systems and certain products against specific regulatory requirements. Designated by national authorities, these organizations are crucial for ensuring that high-risk AI systems comply with relevant regulations and standards. Emphasizing independence, objectivity, and impartiality in their assessment activities, Notified Bodies are dedicated to safeguarding confidentiality and professionalism throughout the evaluation process.

These entities assist providers in meeting regulatory standards by verifying that high-risk AI systems and other products meet necessary criteria for safety and effectiveness before being introduced to the market. Notified Bodies possess legal personality and are committed to conducting thorough conformity assessment activities within their respective fields. Moreover, they ensure that any subcontractors or subsidiaries adhere to the same regulatory requirements.

In summary, Notified Bodies are essential organizations responsible for maintaining safety and regulatory compliance for high-risk AI systems and various products within the EU market. They serve as designated entities responsible for conducting conformity assessments and certifying that products or systems meet established regulatory standards, thereby ensuring compliance with EU quality management system standards and technical documentation requirements.

Member State
A Member State refers to a country that is a part of the European Union (EU) and is integral to the governing body of the union. These Member States are bound by specific regulations and authority protocols that guide their designation, certification, and overarching compliance with EU standards, particularly in sectors involving biometric technologies and high-risk artificial intelligence (AI) systems.

Each Member State is responsible for ensuring adherence to EU regulations by establishing national laws and implementing effective conformity assessment procedures. This includes creating mechanisms for market surveillance that uphold the regulatory framework set by the EU, thus ensuring compliance and safety in AI systems. Member States not only play a crucial role in legislative discussions but also actively participate in the EU's broader political and economic framework.

In addition to their regulatory and compliance responsibilities, Member States determine and provide necessary language and comprehension requirements for AI instructions, thereby establishing standards for language accessibility in AI deployments. As part of their enforcement duties, they also possess the authority to impose administrative fines to ensure compliance.

In summary, Member States are sovereign entities within the European Union that are vital to the implementation and oversight of EU mandates, focusing particularly on emerging technologies and AI systems. They oversee conformity assessment bodies and enforce testing regulations as stipulated by Union legislation, reinforcing their essential role in the collective governance of the EU.<SEP>Member States are countries within a union that notify and regulate the competence of notified bodies.<SEP>A Member State refers to countries that are members of the European Union and adhere to its regulations regarding AI systems certification.

Conformity Assessment Activities
Conformity Assessment Activities are processes conducted by notified bodies to verify and ensure that products, services, or organizations meet the necessary standards and regulations across various sectors. These activities encompass a series of procedures and evaluations that are crucial in determining compliance with established guidelines, particularly for high-risk AI systems. The aim of Conformity Assessment Activities is to assess compliance before certifying products, ensuring that they adhere to the requisite standards and regulations. Through these systematic evaluations, conformity assessment activities play a pivotal role in maintaining safety and regulatory compliance within the marketplace.

Legal Personality
Legal personality refers to the recognition of an organization as a distinct legal entity capable of owning property and being liable for its actions.

Quality Management Requirements

Resource Requirements
Resource requirements encompass the necessary tools, personnel, and infrastructure that notified bodies need to effectively conduct conformity assessments.

Cybersecurity Requirements
Cybersecurity Requirements are standards that products with digital elements, particularly high-risk AI systems, must meet to ensure their resilience and safety against cyber threats.<SEP>Cybersecurity requirements entail measures that notified bodies must implement to protect sensitive information during conformity assessments.

Independence
Independence refers to the need for notified bodies to operate without influence from external parties that may compromise their assessment integrity.

Impartiality
Impartiality signifies the objective and fair conduct of notified bodies during conformity assessments, ensuring unbiased evaluations.

Liability Insurance
Liability Insurance is coverage that protects notified bodies against claims related to their conformity assessment activities.<SEP>Liability insurance is a requirement for notified bodies to mitigate risks associated with the consequences of their assessments.

Article 78
Article 78 establishes specific confidentiality obligations concerning information and documentation obtained during compliance assessments, particularly as they relate to conformity assessment activities. This legal provision ensures that personnel in notified bodies adhere to proper conduct and maintain confidentiality regarding sensitive information. Article 78 also outlines the confidentiality requirements for information acquired by national public authorities under Union law, including details pertinent to high-risk AI systems. Additionally, it specifies the legal elements or requirements that take effect on a predetermined date, reinforcing the importance of safeguarding confidential information in compliance with regulations.<SEP>Article 78 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 pertains to the confidentiality of information obtained during the regulatory compliance process.<SEP>Article 78 pertains to the confidentiality of sensitive information during investigations conducted by the Commission.<SEP>Article 78 refers to a specific provision within EU legislation that mandates confidentiality for information obtained by notified bodies.

European Standardisation Organisations
European Standardisation Organisations are bodies that develop and maintain standards and facilitate coordination among notified bodies regarding assessment activities.<SEP>European Standardisation Organisations are bodies that work towards the development and dissemination of standards across Europe.<SEP>European standardisation organisations develop harmonised standards for various requirements as part of EU regulations.<SEP>European Standardisation Organisations are groups tasked with developing and promoting harmonised standards within the EU.<SEP>European standardisation organisations are responsible for developing and implementing standards within the EU framework, particularly for AI systems and models.

Personnel
Personnel refers to the individuals who perform various roles within an organization or system, often requiring specific expertise.<SEP>Personnel refers to the staff and workforce associated with notified bodies, responsible for carrying out conformity assessment tasks and maintaining professional integrity.

Competence
Competence pertains to the required skills, knowledge, and authority for individuals assigned to implement AI system instructions and conduct oversight.<SEP>Competence refers to the requisite skills and expertise that notified bodies and personnel must possess to effectively evaluate conformity assessments and AI systems.

Technical Personnel
Technical Personnel are individuals with specialized knowledge and skills required to conduct evaluations and assessments in conformity assessment activities.

Scientific Personnel
Scientific Personnel are individuals involved in providing scientific expertise and support for the evaluation of AI systems and data computing.

Legal Personnel
Legal Personnel are individuals with legal expertise who ensure compliance with regulations and handle legal responsibilities in conformity assessments.

Section 2
Section 2 outlines specific requirements that high-risk AI systems must comply with to ensure their safe deployment and use.<SEP>Section 2 refers to a part of the regulation that establishes the requirements that high-risk AI systems must meet for compliance.<SEP>Section 2 refers to a specific part of regulatory text that outlines particular compliance requirements to be adhered to by providers.<SEP>Section 2 refers to a specific part of the regulatory framework established by the European Union, which outlines the necessary requirements that high-risk AI systems must comply with to ensure their safety, efficacy, and conformity. It emphasizes the importance of a conformity assessment process, detailing the standards that such AI systems must meet to be deemed compliant and safe for the market. Additionally, Section 2 addresses requirements related to standardization processes within the EU, ensuring that high-risk AI systems adhere to established guidelines and criteria for their deployment. Overall, this section serves as a critical component of the regulatory framework aimed at regulating high-risk AI technologies effectively.

High-risk AI systems
High-risk AI systems are designed for applications that require human oversight to ensure they function correctly and mitigate negative consequences.<SEP>High-risk AI systems refer to artificial intelligence applications that necessitate compliance with EU regulations due to their potential impact on safety and health, requiring specific certification.<SEP>High-risk AI systems refer to artificial intelligence systems that require stringent design and development protocols to ensure accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity throughout their lifecycle.

Stakeholders and organizations include metrology and benchmarking authorities involved in the measurement and assessment of high-risk AI systems.

Performance Metrics
Performance metrics are measurements that gauge the accuracy and robustness of high-risk AI systems, crucial for their validation and operational use.<SEP>Performance metrics are standards outlined in Article 15 to evaluate the accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity of high-risk AI systems.

Feedback Loops
Feedback loops are processes where outputs from AI systems influence future inputs to improve operations.<SEP>Feedback loops involve processes through which inputs are refined and adjusted based on outputs, requiring monitoring and mitigation strategies.<SEP>Feedback loops refer to the processes by which the output of a high-risk AI system is used to influence future inputs, which must be managed to avoid biased outcomes.<SEP>Feedback loops occur when outputs from AI systems influence future inputs, potentially creating cycles of discrimination or bias if not managed correctly.

Technical Redundancy Solutions
Technical redundancy solutions involve backup systems and fail-safe plans that enhance the resilience of high-risk AI systems against errors and faults.

Unauthorized Third Parties
Unauthorized third parties refer to individuals or groups attempting to exploit vulnerabilities in AI systems for malicious intents.<SEP>Unauthorized third parties represent individuals or entities attempting to exploit vulnerabilities in high-risk AI systems, posing a cybersecurity risk.

Cybersecurity Measures
Cybersecurity Measures are protections put in place to safeguard information and data integrity against unauthorized access or breaches.<SEP>Cybersecurity measures are strategies and practices implemented to protect high-risk AI systems from attacks and unauthorized alterations.<SEP>Cybersecurity measures include techniques and strategies implemented to defend against unauthorized access and attacks on AI systems.<SEP>Cybersecurity Measures are protocols and practices designed to protect data from theft and damage, particularly in the context of high-risk AI systems.

Data Poisoning
Data poisoning is a type of attack where malicious data is introduced to a training set to corrupt the learning process of AI systems.<SEP>Data poisoning refers to attacks that introduce corrupt data into training datasets to manipulate AI outputs.<SEP>Data poisoning refers to attacks that manipulate the training data sets of AI systems, affecting their performance and integrity.

Model Poisoning
Model poisoning involves attacks targeting pre-trained components of AI systems, potentially compromising their reliability and outputs.<SEP>Model poisoning is a vulnerability where business-critical models are compromised by corrupt components used during AI training.

Adversarial Examples
Adversarial examples are inputs designed to deceive an AI model, resulting in incorrect outputs and demonstrating vulnerability.<SEP>Adversarial examples are malicious inputs specifically designed to deceive AI models into making incorrect predictions.

Cybersecurity
Cybersecurity refers to the comprehensive set of practices, measures, and technologies designed to protect computer systems, networks, and data from unauthorized access, attacks, and potential threats. In the context of artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity is especially critical as it focuses on safeguarding high-risk AI systems from unauthorized access and actions that could compromise their integrity, confidentiality, and availability. This includes protecting hardware, software, and data from theft or damage, as well as preventing disruptions in service. Overall, cybersecurity encompasses a range of strategies aimed at defending against digital attacks, thereby ensuring the secure operation of systems and services, particularly those involving artificial intelligence.

operator

The article emphasizes the importance of adhering to specific provisions that delineate these prohibitions in the context of AI development and application. Additionally, Article 5 includes provisions for the European Commission to evaluate and implement necessary updates to the list of prohibited practices, ensuring that regulations remain relevant and effective in managing the evolving landscape of artificial intelligence.<SEP>Article 5 refers to provisions within the regulatory framework that establish prohibitions and restrictions regarding the usage of high-risk AI systems.<SEP>Article 5 specifies prohibitions on certain AI practices, forming a core part of the regulations governing AI usage in the EU.

Real-Time Systems

Providers

Providers can include companies as well as individual developers, and they are responsible for navigating a complex landscape of applicable laws and regulations, particularly concerning high-risk AI technologies and intellectual property rights.

In their efforts to comply with these regulations, Providers create and maintain post-market monitoring systems to oversee the performance and safety of their AI technologies. This ongoing oversight involves reporting incidents and notifying regulatory authorities about their testing processes. Providers also participate in AI regulatory sandboxes, which allow them to test compliance and engage in innovative practices within a controlled environment, thereby helping to meet safety and performance standards.

Overall, Providers are essential to the regulatory framework surrounding AI technologies, working diligently to foster safe, compliant, and innovative AI systems. They play a crucial role in ensuring the effective use of AI systems while also being obligated to report any associated risks. Overall, Deployers are tasked with not only deploying these technologies but also with adhering to applicable regulations to ensure safe and responsible use.<SEP>Deployers are individuals or organizations that implement high-risk AI systems and require appropriate training and instructions to use them effectively.<SEP>Deployers are organizations or individuals responsible for the implementation and management of AI systems, ensuring they meet regulatory standards.<SEP>Deployers are the individuals or organizations responsible for implementing high-risk AI systems and must ensure adherence to relevant standards and guidelines.

Board
The Board is a comprehensive governing body integral to the oversight and implementation of regulations related to artificial intelligence (AI) within the European Union. It represents diverse interests within the AI ecosystem, facilitating the effective implementation of AI regulations through various advisory tasks. The Board possesses the authority to form both standing and temporary sub-groups to delve into specific regulatory issues, allowing for detailed discussions and informed decisions on complex matters.

Furthermore, the Board participates in decision-making processes related to market surveillance, empowered to formally request actions from the AI Office to implement the regulatory framework. It also oversees communications concerning penalties imposed under AI regulations, receiving information on these fines as part of its regulatory oversight responsibilities.

In addition to its regulatory functions, the Board offers guidance and support to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and start-ups, helping them navigate compliance with regulations. AI Value Chain
AI Value Chain refers to the series of processes involved in designing, developing, deploying, and managing AI systems, where responsibilities must be clearly defined.<SEP>The AI Value Chain refers to the series of processes and entities involved in the development, implementation, and regulation of artificial intelligence technologies.<SEP>The AI value chain represents the various stages of developing and deploying artificial intelligence systems, emphasizing responsibilities of different stakeholders.<SEP>The AI Value Chain encompasses all parties and processes involved in the development and deployment of AI systems, tools, and services.<SEP>The AI value chain encompasses the various stages and processes involved in the development and deployment of artificial intelligence systems, highlighting the interconnections between different stakeholders such as providers and users of AI models.

Risk-Management System
A risk-management system for AI should be a continuous and iterative process aimed at identifying and mitigating risks associated with AI systems.<SEP>A risk-management system is a structured approach to identifying, assessing, and mitigating risks associated with high-risk AI systems.

Compliance Requirements
Compliance Requirements are the mandatory standards and regulations that products, especially those related to high-risk AI systems, must meet to be legally available in the Union market.<SEP>Compliance requirements are the established standards and guidelines that AI systems must adhere to in order to ensure safety, reliability, and accountability.<SEP>Compliance requirements are the standards and guidelines that must be followed to ensure that high-risk AI systems and medical devices function safely and effectively.<SEP>Compliance requirements are the standards and guidelines that AI systems must meet to ensure safety and effectiveness.

Lifetime of AI Systems
The lifetime of AI systems encompasses all phases from development to retirement, during which performance, compliance, and safety must be continuously monitored.

Events and Logs

Union Level
Union Level is a reference to the broader regulatory environment across member states where systemic risks associated with AI models must be addressed.<SEP>Union Level refers to the legislative and regulatory framework governing AI systems, specifically in the context of market surveillance and compliance.<SEP>Union level refers to the collective governance structure at which the regulations and codes of practice are enforced.<SEP>Union Level refers to the collective level of governance or decision-making within the Union related to transparency and AI content detection.<SEP>Union Level refers to the centralized governance and decision-making structure within the European Union regarding the regulation and implementation of AI policies.

Providers of High-Risk AI Systems
Providers of high-risk AI systems are entities tasked with the critical responsibility of ensuring that their AI technologies comply with applicable regulations and safety standards. These organizations must adhere to relevant regulations concerning the operation and management of AI systems, particularly those characterized by significant potential risks to users and society. They are responsible for designing and developing AI technologies that are classified as high-risk, akin to the operations of financial institutions and other regulated entities. Additionally, providers must demonstrate conformity with established requirements when requested by competent authorities, ensuring accountability and compliance in their deployment of AI systems in the market. Timely adherence to deadlines for regulatory compliance is also a key duty of these providers, highlighting their role in maintaining both safety and legal standards in the field of artificial intelligence.<SEP>Providers of high-risk AI systems refers to organizations or individuals that develop or deploy artificial intelligence technologies that pose significant risks and require specialized contractual terms.

This document is especially important for high-risk AI systems, which are required to provide the EU Declaration of Conformity as proof of compliance with specific regulations. By ensuring that products align with EU standards, the Declaration plays a vital role in maintaining safety and regulatory adherence within the European market.<SEP>The EU Declaration of Conformity is a document affirming that a product meets the necessary regulatory standards and requirements.<SEP>The EU Declaration of Conformity is a document issued that certifies that a product meets the required standards, including cybersecurity requirements for high-risk AI systems.<SEP>The EU Declaration of Conformity is a document that confirms a product's compliance with EU regulations and directives.

A Quality Management System is a structured system of processes and procedures required to ensure that high-risk AI systems comply with relevant regulations and standards.<SEP>A quality management system is a structured system of procedures and responsibilities necessary for the management of quality within an organization.<SEP>A quality management system is a structured framework aimed at ensuring consistent quality in products and services, particularly in high-risk sectors.
