United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities
The United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities is an international human rights treaty aimed at protecting the rights and dignity of persons with disabilities.

Directive (EU) 2016/2102
Directive (EU) 2016/2102 is a legal framework established for ensuring the accessibility of websites and mobile applications of public sector bodies in the EU.

Directive (EU) 2019/882
Directive (EU) 2019/882 is a legislative measure enacted by the European Parliament and Council that establishes harmonized rules for the accessibility of products and services within the European Union. It aims to ensure compliance with its requirements by making products available on the market and regulating the accessibility, availability, and usability of information related to these products in the EU database.

The directive is particularly focused on ensuring that products and services are accessible to persons with disabilities, thereby promoting inclusivity and equal opportunities. It also outlines specific accessibility requirements that affect consumer rights and protections, demonstrating a commitment to creating a safe and equitable environment for all users. 

Furthermore, Directive (EU) 2019/882 aims to provide a high level of protection against harmful artificial intelligence systems and regulates AI practices to prevent the distortion of human behavior, especially for vulnerable groups. Overall, the directive underscores the EU's dedication to safeguarding rights and ensuring that all consumers, regardless of their abilities, can access and benefit from available products and services.

AI Technologies
AI Technologies refer to various advanced technologies involving artificial intelligence, including data computing and automation systems, which are regulated by competent authorities.<SEP>AI Technologies refers to systems and tools based on artificial intelligence that require compliance with accessibility standards to serve all users effectively.<SEP>AI technologies refer to advanced systems that utilize artificial intelligence, categorized as high-risk based on their potential impact.<SEP>AI technologies encompass advancements in artificial intelligence which are crucial for the competence and functioning of the national authorities.

Persons with Disabilities
Persons with Disabilities refers to individuals who have long-term physical, mental, intellectual, or sensory impairments that may hinder their full and effective participation in society on an equal basis with others.<SEP>Persons with Disabilities represent a demographic that could benefit from AI solutions designed to enhance accessibility and inclusion.<SEP>Persons with disabilities are individuals with physical or mental impairments that may limit their full participation in society and require specific attention and accessibility measures.

SMEs
SMEs (Small and Medium-sized Enterprises) are a category of businesses that have specific interests and needs regarding the regulation of AI systems.<SEP>Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs) are crucial components of the economy, recognized for their significant contributions as providers or deployers of artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Defined by having a limited number of employees and specific turnover thresholds, SMEs encompass businesses that often include start-ups. Due to their relatively constrained resources, SMEs are frequently the focus of regulatory frameworks aimed at fostering innovation and promoting economic growth.

To support SMEs in meeting these challenges, they benefit from free access to AI regulatory sandboxes, which provide a controlled environment for testing and developing AI technologies. These sandboxes are designed to facilitate innovation while minimizing the regulatory burdens that SMEs face. Additionally, SMEs are encouraged to participate in the development of standards in accordance with EU regulations, highlighting their importance as stakeholders in the regulatory process.

When navigating compliance with various regulations, SMEs are able to provide technical documentation in a simplified manner, which addresses specific certification and compliance costs they encounter. This approach aims to alleviate the economic strain on these enterprises, which may otherwise face potential fines or regulatory pressures related to their operations in the AI sector. Overall, SMEs play a vital role in shaping the landscape of AI innovation, and regulatory guidelines increasingly consider their unique challenges and contributions.<SEP>Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) play a vital role in the advisory forum, representing commercial interests and innovation.<SEP>SMEs, or Small and Medium-sized Enterprises, benefit from simplified compliance methods that aim to reduce costs associated with regulatory obligations concerning AI models.<SEP>Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs) are included as part of the commercial interests represented in the advisory forum.

Start-ups
Start-ups are a subset of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) characterized by their innovative nature and a focus on technology, particularly in the area of artificial intelligence (AI). These newly established businesses often aim to create innovative products or services and are typically in the early stages of development. As part of efforts to support their growth and compliance, start-ups have access to AI regulatory sandboxes, which provide them with free resources to test and navigate various regulatory requirements related to AI deployment. Moreover, start-ups play a crucial role in the innovation landscape and are represented among various stakeholders in advisory forums dedicated to addressing regulatory issues. Their need for support in navigating these regulations is essential for fostering their development and ensuring successful integration of their innovations into the market.

Conformity Assessment Fees
Conformity Assessment Fees are charges assessed for the evaluation of compliance with regulations, significant for SMEs.<SEP>Conformity Assessment Fees are the costs associated with ensuring compliance with the Regulation, which may be reduced for SMEs based on their size and market situation.<SEP>Conformity Assessment Fees relate to costs that SMEs incur for ensuring their AI systems comply with regulatory requirements.

Training Activities
Training Activities refer to specific programs organized to raise awareness and educate SMEs and start-ups about the application of the Regulation.

Standardisation Development Process
The Standardisation Development Process is the procedure by which SMEs and relevant stakeholders participate in the formulation of standards related to AI.

Operators
Operators are individuals or organizations responsible for deploying and managing AI systems, subject to compliance with regulations and obligations.<SEP>Operators are the entities or individuals that will utilize AI systems and are affected by the obligations arising from the Regulation.<SEP>Operators encompass individuals or entities involved in the AI value chain, including importers and distributors, responsible for various roles and obligations.<SEP>Operators refer to entities or individuals managing or overseeing the implementation and functioning of high-risk AI systems.

Information Platform

Standardised Templates
Standardised Templates are pre-defined documents provided by the Commission to assist SMEs and start-ups in meeting regulatory requirements.<SEP>Standardised Templates are pre-set documents intended to help SMEs navigate regulation compliance upon request.<SEP>Standardised templates are predefined formats created by the AI Office to facilitate compliance with the Regulation, ensuring uniformity for operators.

EU Database
The EU Database is a centralized and secure repository established by the European Commission to register and track high-risk AI systems in accordance with European Union regulations. It plays a crucial role in ensuring compliance with product standards and provides essential support for regulatory processes. This database not only documents the registration of AI systems but also facilitates the management and regulation of data related to law enforcement practices across Member States.

Under specific regulations outlined in the EU legal framework, providers are mandated to register high-risk AI systems within the EU Database. This repository contains detailed records and specifications, including sections and annexes that pertain to the relevant legal articles, ensuring comprehensive oversight and adherence to compliance in the deployment of AI technologies within the Union.

Furthermore, the EU Database serves as an informational repository monitored by regulatory authorities, where data regarding the compliance and evaluation of AI systems is stored. It is also identified in regulations as a source of information for market surveillance authorities to check compliance concerning AI systems. Overall, the EU Database is an official system instrumental in regulatory compliance and data management related to high-risk AI technologies within the European Union.

Non-Compliance
Non-Compliance refers to the failure to meet regulatory requirements, which can trigger actions by the market surveillance authority against providers.

High-Risk AI System Compliance
High-Risk AI System Compliance involves the legal and regulatory processes ensuring that AI systems categorized as high-risk meet strict safety and operational standards.<SEP>High-risk AI system compliance refers to the adherence to regulatory standards and corrective actions necessary when a system does not conform to these standards.

National Market Surveillance Authorities
National Market Surveillance Authorities are responsible for monitoring market activities to ensure compliance with laws and regulations related to product safety and consumer protection.<SEP>National Market Surveillance Authorities are responsible for supervising AI systems at the national level, particularly in cases where the AI system is not high-risk or does not involve overlapping competences with the AI Office.<SEP>National market surveillance authorities monitor compliance with laws and regulations regarding market practices in Member States.

Compliance Evaluations
Compliance Evaluations are assessments conducted to ensure that AI systems meet established legal and regulatory standards.<SEP>Compliance evaluations are assessments conducted to determine if AI systems adhere to the regulatory obligations required for high-risk classifications.

Cross-Border Cases
Cross-Border Cases pertain to regulatory situations that involve multiple jurisdictions and require cooperation among authorities.

Mutatis Mutandis

legal acts

technical progress
Technical progress refers to advancements or improvements in technology that may necessitate changes in documentation and compliance requirements.

scientific panel
The scientific panel consists of experts that Member States can call upon for support in enforcing regulations.<SEP>The scientific panel is a group of independent experts established to provide expertise and support for the implementation of AI regulations.<SEP>The scientific panel is an independent group of experts established under Article 68, tasked with advising the Commission on the classification of AI models based on their systemic risk and compliance with regulations. Comprised of knowledgeable professionals, the panel performs assessments and evaluations of general-purpose AI models, ensuring impartiality and confidentiality throughout its tasks. In addition to offering insights, the scientific panel is responsible for issuing alerts regarding potential risks posed by AI models and supporting the effective implementation of AI regulations.<SEP>The scientific panel supports governance systems for AI and monitors risks associated with general-purpose AI models.

Article 90
Article 90 outlines the obligations and responsibilities regarding the identification of systemic risks associated with AI models at the Union level.<SEP>Article 90 provides details on the procedures and criteria for alerts about risks associated with AI models.<SEP>Article 90 refers to a policy or guideline regarding the development and regulation of general-purpose AI models within a legal framework.

Article 68

Independent Experts
Independent Experts are individuals selected to evaluate AI models, ensuring unbiased assessment and adherence to legal standards in AI implementation.<SEP>Independent experts are professionals or academics who provide objective insights and recommendations in the regulation process.<SEP>Independent experts are individuals engaged by the AI Office to conduct evaluations and ensure compliance with the Regulation.

Internal Testing
Internal Testing refers to the procedures and assessments conducted within the provider's organization to ensure the AI model's functionality and safety prior to external evaluations.

Systemic Risks
Systemic Risks refer to the potential hazards and vulnerabilities associated with the implementation and deployment of General-Purpose AI Models. These risks have the capacity to significantly impact society, markets, and broader systems, thereby necessitating regulatory oversight and careful management. Key areas of concern include public health, safety, and societal structures, where the adverse effects of such AI models may manifest.

The concept of Systemic Risks encompasses various threats that can emerge from the design and functioning of AI systems, which may lead to serious incidents and widespread negative consequences across multiple stakeholders. As a result, there is a pronounced need for comprehensive identification, assessment, and management of these risks, as well as the establishment of a robust regulatory framework to recognize and address potential hazards effectively. Overall, Systemic Risks highlight the importance of vigilance and proactive measures in the effective governance of AI technologies to safeguard against their inherent dangers.<SEP>Systemic risks refer to the potential widespread impacts and threats associated with failures in AI systems, which the AI Office must monitor and mitigate.<SEP>Systemic risks are potential threats posed by AI models that could lead to significant societal or economic impacts.

Evaluations
Evaluations refer to the formal processes undertaken to assess the compliance and safety of the general-purpose AI models, involving various stakeholders.

Union or Member State law
Union or Member State law provides the legal framework under which biometric data processing for law enforcement can be authorized and regulated.

Article 10
Article 10 of Directive (EU) 2016/680 pertains to the safeguards required for the processing of personal data.<SEP>Article 10 of Directive (EU) 2016/680 specifies conditions under which biometric data processing is necessary for law enforcement, emphasizing the need for appropriate safeguards.

Article 4 (1)
Article 4 (1) of Directive (EU) 2016/680 outlines principles such as lawfulness, fairness, and transparency that must be respected during the processing of biometric data.

AI Ecosystem
The AI Ecosystem refers to the interconnected environment in which AI technologies are developed, implemented, and regulated, involving various stakeholders and authorities.<SEP>The AI Ecosystem refers to the network of actors involved in the development, implementation, and regulation of artificial intelligence technologies.

Regulatory Framework
Regulatory Framework refers to the overarching set of laws and regulations governing the development and use of artificial intelligence systems within the EU.<SEP>The Regulatory Framework encompasses the laws and regulations governing the establishment and operation of AI regulatory sandboxes.<SEP>The Regulatory Framework outlines the rules and guidelines governing the establishment and operation of AI sandboxes, ensuring responsible innovation.<SEP>The regulatory framework refers to the comprehensive set of laws and guidelines governing the deployment and utilization of AI technologies and systems.<SEP>The regulatory framework establishes the rules and guidelines for the operation, reporting, and oversight of AI systems in the EU.

Established by national competent authorities, AI Regulatory Sandboxes provide a structured framework for the experimentation of AI technologies under regulatory supervision. They allow for testing in real-world conditions, alleviating legal and administrative burdens, and promoting competitiveness within the industry. Overall, AI Regulatory Sandboxes play a crucial role in facilitating the responsible advancement of artificial intelligence by balancing innovation with regulatory compliance.<SEP>AI Regulatory Sandboxes are frameworks within which AI technologies can be tested in real-world conditions under regulatory oversight.<SEP>AI Regulatory Sandboxes are controlled environments designed to foster innovation in artificial intelligence by allowing developers to test and experiment with AI systems while ensuring compliance with regulations.<SEP>AI Regulatory Sandboxes refer to controlled environments established to allow for the testing and development of artificial intelligence systems while ensuring compliance with relevant regulations and standards.

Data Protection Authorities
Data Protection Authorities are regulatory bodies that ensure the protection of personal data and privacy rights within their jurisdictions in relation to AI systems.<SEP>Data Protection Authorities oversee the enforcement of data protection laws and ensure that personal data is handled in accordance with regulations.<SEP>Data Protection Authorities are specific public bodies that oversee and ensure compliance with data protection regulations.

Conformity Assessment Process

Commission and the Board
The Commission and the Board are regulatory bodies responsible for the oversight and governance of AI systems within the framework of European Union regulations.

Cross-Border Cooperation
Cross-Border Cooperation refers to collaborative efforts between different national competent authorities to facilitate the regulation and supervision of AI systems across borders.

National Data Protection Authorities
National Data Protection Authorities are regulatory bodies responsible for overseeing the processing of personal data and ensuring compliance with data protection laws.<SEP>National data protection authorities oversee the enforcement of data protection laws and make sure that personal data is handled correctly in Member States.<SEP>National Data Protection Authorities are responsible for enforcing data protection laws and have the power to issue prohibition decisions on biometric data processing.

The AI Regulatory Sandbox Project is an initiative designed for testing innovative AI applications in a controlled regulatory environment.

Profiling

Risk Assessments
Risk Assessments are evaluations conducted using AI systems to predict the likelihood of a natural person committing a criminal offense based on their behavior.<SEP>Risk assessments evaluate the potential risks associated with individuals based on specific behaviours or characteristics, typically employed in legal contexts.<SEP>Risk assessments in AI involve evaluating the potential impacts and safety of AI systems concerning individual rights and public safety.

Additionally, the European Council works collaboratively with the European Parliament to establish policies and regulations, including notable frameworks such as Regulation (EU) 2019/881 and the Data Act. Through its legislative involvement, the European Council ensures that the EU's political framework is aligned with the collective interests and goals of its member states, reinforcing its pivotal position in shaping European policies and legislation.<SEP>The European Council is responsible for setting the EU's overall political direction and priorities, working closely with the European Parliament on legislative matters.<SEP>The European Council is an institution of the European Union that defines the general political direction and priorities, contributing to legislation like Regulation (EU) 2023/988.

prohibited practices
Prohibited practices refer to specific uses of AI systems that are deemed unacceptable and are banned under the regulation to ensure safety and ethical standards.

energy-efficient development
Energy-efficient development refers to the methodologies and practices aimed at reducing energy consumption in the design and operation of AI systems.

AI Regulations
AI Regulations refer to the legal frameworks established to oversee the development, implementation, and testing of AI technologies while ensuring safety and compliance.<SEP>AI Regulations refer to the set of rules and standards implemented to govern the development and use of artificial intelligence technology.

Risk Mitigation Measures
Risk Mitigation Measures are strategies and protocols put in place to minimize potential risks associated with the implementation of AI technologies.

Regulatory Oversight
Regulatory Oversight refers to the mechanisms and processes used by authorities to ensure compliance with laws and safety standards in the development of AI systems.

Model Lifecycle
The model lifecycle encompasses the various stages through which an AI model progresses, influencing its security and risk management practices.

Union Legal Framework
The Union legal framework involves regulations on AI to ensure protection of public interests and support a market for AI systems in the internal market.

Public Interests
Public Interests refer to the collective concerns and welfare of society, particularly in health, safety, and fundamental rights.<SEP>Public interests include health, safety, democracy, and environmental protection which the AI regulation aims to safeguard.<SEP>Public interests encompass the welfare and well-being of the general population, which can be threatened by technological advancements such as AI.

Digital Transformation
Digital transformation refers to the process of integrating digital technologies across all regions of the Union, facilitated by new AI regulations.

Internal Market
The Internal Market is a fundamental aspect of the European Union that allows goods, services, capital, and people to move freely among Member States.<SEP>The Internal Market refers to the integrated economy of the European Union, allowing free movement of goods, services, capital, and people among member states.<SEP>The internal market refers to the regulatory environment that allows for the free movement of goods and services within the European Union, aiming to create a unified economic space.

Startups
Startups are newly established businesses, typically in the technology sector, that are in the early stages of operations and may require supportive regulations to thrive.

Regulations
Regulations encompass the rules and directives that are subject to reporting under Directive (EU) 2019/1937, ensuring compliance and accountability within organizations.<SEP>Regulations refer to the specific rules established by governing bodies like the European Union to manage and oversee the usage of AI technology and ensure compliance with ethical standards.

Harmonised Rules
Harmonised Rules refer to the standardized regulations that govern the market and usage of high-risk AI systems across EU member states, ensuring consistency and safety.<SEP>Harmonised rules are standardized regulations created within the EU framework to ensure consistency and coherence in the application of laws among member states.

Ethical AI
Ethical AI involves the principles guiding the responsible development and use of artificial intelligence technologies, ensuring they align with values such as fairness and accountability.

data.entity_name: Special meeting of the European Council
data.content:
Special meeting of the European Council
The Special meeting of the European Council held on October 1 and 2, 2020, was focused on discussions and conclusions about important EU matters.

20 October 2020
The date signifies a resolution passed by the European Parliament concerning ethical aspects of artificial intelligence and robotics.

European Parliament resolution of 20 October 2020
The resolution passed by the European Parliament on 20 October 2020 contains recommendations related to ethical aspects of artificial intelligence, robotics, and related technologies, influencing policy and regulation.

ethical aspects of artificial intelligence
Ethical aspects of artificial intelligence encompass guidelines and recommendations aimed at ensuring AI technologies are developed and deployed responsibly and ethically.

robotics
Robotics refers to the technology involved in the design, construction, operation, and use of robots, which raises ethical considerations and regulatory challenges.

Regulation (EU) 2022/2065
Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 establishes comprehensive obligations and requirements for providers of AI systems and models operating within the European Union. It focuses particularly on those offering intermediary services, ensuring they have measures in place for the detection and disclosure of outputs that are artificially generated or manipulated. The regulation emphasizes a technology-neutral approach, applying to various AI systems used as intermediary services. Furthermore, it governs the liability of these service providers, detailing the legal obligations they must adhere to. This regulation is closely linked to the Digital Services Act, which aims to create a safer digital environment in the EU while addressing the responsibilities of intermediary service providers.<SEP>Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 outlines obligations for providers of certain AI systems to ensure transparency in outputs that are artificially generated or manipulated.

Online Search Engines
Online search engines are digital tools that retrieve and rank information from various websites based on user queries.

Chatbots
Chatbots are AI-driven applications that simulate human conversation, often providing automated responses in user interactions.

Digital Services
Digital Services encompass online platforms and applications that require regulatory oversight during their operation and integration in the market.<SEP>Digital services refer to online applications and platforms that deliver functionality to users, often utilizing AI technology to improve efficiency and user experience.

Intermediary Services
Intermediary services are platforms or systems that facilitate interactions or transactions between users or entities, often involving the use of AI systems.<SEP>Intermediary services include platforms and services that facilitate interactions or transactions between parties, potentially impacted by regulations on AI.

Knowledge Base
A knowledge base is a system or repository that collects and organizes information, enabling AI systems to retrieve and present relevant data efficiently.

Integration
Integration describes the process of combining various AI components to create a cohesive system that can operate effectively across different domains.

Variety of Purposes
The concept of Variety of Purposes denotes the capability of a general-purpose AI system to serve multiple functions and applications within various fields.

Law-Enforcement Authorities
Law-Enforcement Authorities are responsible for maintaining public order and safety, and may deploy high-risk AI systems in urgent situations.

Civil Protection Authorities
Civil Protection Authorities focus on protecting citizens from emergencies and disasters and may also use AI systems.<SEP>Civil protection authorities are tasked with protecting citizens and may also deploy high-risk AI systems in emergencies.

Life and Health Protection
Life and Health Protection deals with safeguarding individuals' health and safety, especially in decision-making related to AI usage.

EU Member States
EU Member States are countries that are part of the European Union and are involved in the regulatory process for high-risk AI systems.<SEP>EU Member States refer to the countries that are part of the European Union and are involved in establishing regulations and protocols regarding AI systems.

Objection Period
The Objection Period is the timeframe within which Member States can raise objections to the authorization of high-risk AI systems.

Public Security or Protection
Public security or protection encompasses the measures taken to safeguard the wellbeing of individuals, which may influence the deployment of AI systems.

Substantial and Imminent Threat
A Substantial and Imminent Threat refers to an urgent risk that necessitates the immediate use of high-risk AI systems by law enforcement or civil protection authorities.

High-Risk AI System Authorization
High-Risk AI System Authorization is the approval process required for deploying high-risk AI systems, ensuring they comply with safety regulations.

Operational Data
Operational Data refers to sensitive information pertaining to the activities of law enforcement authorities that is excluded from certain obligations.

Objectivity
Objectivity refers to the principle that national competent authorities must safeguard in their activities, ensuring decisions are made without personal bias.

Confidentiality Rules
Confidentiality Rules are guidelines that govern the conduct of the members of national competent authorities regarding the handling of sensitive information.

Members of Authorities
Members of Authorities are individuals who serve in national competent authorities and must adhere to the principles and rules laid out in the Regulation.

AI Solutions
AI Solutions encompass various technologies and methodologies in artificial intelligence aimed at improving social and environmental outcomes.

Socio-Economic Inequalities
Socio-Economic Inequalities refer to disparities in wealth, resources, and opportunities among different social groups.

Environmental Targets
Environmental Targets set specific goals that AI solutions can help achieve in relation to sustainability and ecological preservation.

Public and Union Funding
Public and Union Funding are financial resources allocated by governments and unions to support AI-related research and development.

Research and Development
Research and Development refers to the systematic work undertaken to innovate and introduce new products or processes, particularly in AI solutions aimed at societal benefits.

Interdisciplinary Cooperation
Interdisciplinary Cooperation involves collaboration among various fields and disciplines to address complex issues such as accessibility and inequality through AI.

AI Developers
AI Developers are individuals or teams who create and advance artificial intelligence technologies and applications.

Experts on Inequality
Experts on Inequality are professionals specializing in the analysis and resolution of socio-economic disparities and their impacts on society.

Accessibility
Accessibility refers to the design of products, devices, services, or environments for people with disabilities.

Consumer Rights
Consumer Rights are the legal protections and entitlements consumers have in the market, including equitable treatment and safety.

Digital Rights
Digital Rights pertain to freedoms and protections related to digital technology and its use, ensuring fairness and access to digital services.

Civil Society Organisations
Civil Society Organisations are involved as stakeholders in the formation of standards and codes of conduct for AI systems.<SEP>Civil society organisations are stakeholders that may participate in supporting the process of developing codes of practice for AI.

General-Purpose AI Models Providers
Providers of general-purpose AI models are invited to contribute to the creation of codes of practice, ensuring that their operations align with regulations.

Articles 53 and 55
Articles 53 and 55 refer to specific provisions in the regulation that outline obligations for AI practices and codes.

International Approaches
International approaches refer to best practices and standards developed globally for the regulation and use of AI systems.<SEP>International approaches refer to the global standards and practices that the AI Office considers while drawing up codes of practice.<SEP>International approaches signify collaborative efforts among nations to address the ethical and practical concerns surrounding the development and deployment of AI technologies.

Codes of Practice
Codes of practice are guidelines designed to ensure ethical and safe development and use of AI models, taking into account diverse perspectives and international standards.<SEP>Codes of practice are guidelines developed at the Union level to manage the obligations and ensure the safe use of AI technologies.<SEP>Codes of practice are guidelines established to ensure ethical and safe use of AI technologies by providers, aimed at mitigating risks.<SEP>Codes of practice function as guidelines for providers of AI models to demonstrate compliance with the obligations set forth in the Regulation.

Civil Society Organizations
Civil society organizations are groups that advocate for public interests and provide diverse perspectives in the development of codes for AI models.<SEP>Civil society organizations are non-governmental entities that represent the interests of the public and may contribute to the development of AI regulations.

codes of practice
Codes of practice are guidelines developed to facilitate compliance with obligations related to AI-generated or manipulated content.<SEP>Codes of practice are regulatory frameworks that set specific objectives, commitments, and performance indicators for stakeholders involved in AI development and implementation.

general-purpose AI models
General-purpose AI models are types of artificial intelligence designed for a wide range of tasks and may be subject to regulatory scrutiny.<SEP>General-purpose AI models are versatile AI constructs that can be employed across various applications and sectors.<SEP>General-purpose AI models are versatile artificial intelligence systems designed to perform a wide range of tasks and can be adapted for various applications. These models are intended for broad usage and are subject to oversight under specific regulations. Providers of general-purpose AI models have obligations regarding their technical documentation, which ensures transparency and accountability. Due to their high-impact capabilities, these models present associated systemic risks that need to be managed effectively. The evaluation and oversight of these models are conducted by entities such as the AI Office and a scientific panel, reflecting their importance and the need for responsible governance in their deployment.<SEP>General-purpose AI models refer to AI models that can be used for various purposes and are subject to specific regulatory compliance.<SEP>General-purpose AI models refer to AI systems that can perform a wide variety of tasks and are subject to specific governance and monitoring activities.

civil society organizations
Civil society organizations are various groups representing the interests of individuals and communities, contributing to the development of codes of practice and advocacy for stakeholder needs.

industry
The industry includes businesses and organizations involved in developing, deploying, and utilizing general-purpose AI models.<SEP>The industry represents businesses and enterprises that engage in AI development and application, playing a critical role in adhering to codes of practice and regulatory measures.

academia
Academia refers to educational institutions and researchers involved in studying and setting standards for AI, influencing the codes of practice through research and expertise.<SEP>Academia represents educational institutions that are involved in research and development relevant to AI and data exchange.

downstream providers
Downstream providers are entities that use AI systems developed by others, needing to align their practices with established codes of practice for safety and compliance.

independent experts
Independent experts are individuals with up-to-date scientific or technical expertise in the field of AI, selected to provide objective assessments and recommendations.<SEP>Independent experts are professionals with no vested interests, brought in to provide objective assessments regarding the impact of AI systems.<SEP>Independent experts are specialists or authorities in the field of AI who provide insights and evaluations about the effectiveness and safety of AI practices in relation to the codes.

affected persons
Affected persons are individuals who may be impacted by AI technologies and practices, whose needs and interests must be considered in the development of codes of practice.

key performance indicators
Key performance indicators are measurable values that demonstrate how effectively organizations are achieving their objectives set in the codes of practice.<SEP>Key performance indicators are measurable values used to assess the achievement of objectives and effectiveness of initiatives in various contexts.

Article 98(2)
Article 98(2) provides a comprehensive framework for the examination procedure involved in adopting implementing acts concerning obligations related to artificial intelligence (AI) standards. It outlines specific guidelines governed by EU law that the Commission must follow when making decisions, particularly in relation to the examination of implementing acts associated with the regulation of AI systems and notified bodies. This article serves as a critical provision within the relevant legislation, delineating the procedural steps required for the effective implementation of these obligations.

2 May 2025
2 May 2025 is the deadline by which the codes of practice for AI model providers are expected to be ready.

2 August 2025
2 August 2025 is the date by which the AI Office must finalize the code of practice or assess its adequacy.<SEP>2 August 2025 is the deadline for Member States to communication the identity of testing and market surveillance authorities and publish necessary contacts.<SEP>2 August 2025 is the effective date for the implementation of the provisions on penalties within the Regulation.<SEP>2 August 2025 marks the deadline by which providers must comply with specific regulatory obligations regarding AI models.

Article 98
Article 98 refers to a specific section within a legal or regulatory document that outlines procedures for implementing acts.

Article 2
Article 2 outlines the specific issues that must be addressed in accordance with legal or regulatory frameworks.

High-Risk AI Systems Reporting
High-Risk AI Systems Reporting refers to the mandated process through which providers report serious incidents related to AI systems to authorities.

Causal Link
Causal Link describes the necessary connection established between a high-risk AI system and a serious incident, which is critical for reporting.

Death of a Person
Death of a Person, in this context, pertains to serious incidents involving high-risk AI systems that could lead to fatalities.

Initial Report
Initial Report allows providers to submit incomplete information about serious incidents while they gather more data for a complete report.

Competent Authorities Involvement
Competent Authorities Involvement refers to the participation of designated bodies during investigations of serious incidents related to AI systems.

Regulations (EU) 2019/1020
Regulations (EU) 2019/1020 establish rules for market surveillance concerning products, including the handling of notifications related to serious incidents of AI systems in the European market.

Article 3
Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 specifies definitions and key terms related to high-risk AI systems, including the notification requirements for serious incidents.<SEP>Article 3 outlines specific obligations and procedures related to the reporting of serious incidents in AI systems within the regulatory framework.

Regulations (EU) 2017/745 and (EU) 2017/746
Regulations (EU) 2017/745 and (EU) 2017/746 pertain to the safety and performance of medical devices, relevant for AI systems classified as safety components.

Serious Incidents
Serious incidents refer to significant failures or malfunctions that occur in high-risk AI systems, which must be reported to authorities per the regulations.

Reporting Deployer
The reporting deployer is an entity that operates or uses the high-risk AI system and is involved in reporting risks and compliance issues.

Distributors
Distributors are entities responsible for distributing AI systems within the Union.<SEP>Distributors are entities that handle the logistics of distributing high-risk AI systems to the market, and they need to be informed of compliance status.<SEP>Distributors are operators that supply AI systems to consumers and must comply with legal obligations associated with their role in the value chain.<SEP>Distributors are responsible for the distribution of products and must comply with relevant regulatory requirements.

Market Surveillance
Market surveillance is the process by which regulatory bodies monitor and ensure compliance of products, including technologies, with safety and performance standards.<SEP>Market surveillance is the system of monitoring and regulating high-risk AI systems to ensure they meet safety and compliance standards.

Article 79(1)
Article 79(1) outlines conditions under which high-risk AI systems may present a risk, necessitating careful monitoring and logging practices.<SEP>Article 79(1) outlines specific obligations for providers regarding risk management in high-risk AI systems, mandating timely action upon risk identification.<SEP>Article 79(1) pertains to the legal framework governing the compliance and regulatory obligations associated with high-risk AI systems.

Article 44
Article 44 relates to the requirements for high-risk AI systems, particularly about conformity assessments made by notified bodies.

European Data Protection Regulation
The European Data Protection Regulation sets the legislative framework for data protection across the European Union, mandating how personal data should be handled by organizations.

Affected Persons
Affected persons are individuals located within the Union whose rights may be impacted by the use of AI systems.<SEP>Affected persons are individuals whose rights may have been violated due to an infringement of data protection laws.<SEP>Affected persons are individuals or groups who suffer harm or damages as a result of regulatory infringements and are considered when determining administrative fines.<SEP>Affected persons are individuals who may be significantly impacted by decisions made based on high-risk AI systems, particularly regarding their legal rights, health, safety, and fundamental freedoms.

Technical Measures
Technical Measures are actions or protocols that deployers must take to ensure the safe operation of AI systems, addressing potential risks associated with their deployment.<SEP>Technical measures refer to the organizational controls and technological safeguards implemented by Union institutions to ensure compliance with data protection laws.<SEP>Technical measures refer to the systems and methods implemented by operators to prevent legal infringements and mitigate their impacts.<SEP>Technical measures refer to strategies and implementations aimed at ensuring the robustness and safe operation of high-risk AI systems to prevent undesirable outcomes.

Organizational Measures
Organizational measures involve policies and practices put in place to manage compliance with data protection regulations.<SEP>Organizational measures pertain to the frameworks and guidelines set within organizations to manage risks associated with high-risk AI systems, aimed at enhancing safety and operational integrity.

European Data Protection Supervisor's Opportunity to Be Heard
The European Data Protection Supervisor's Opportunity to Be Heard is a procedural right allowing Union institutions to defend themselves against claims of infringement.

data.entity_name: Union institution, body, office or agency
data.content:
Union institution, body, office or agency
A generic term referring to any official entity within the European Union, including various institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies involved in governance and regulatory frameworks.

data.entity_name: AI Practices referred to in Article 5
data.content:
AI Practices referred to in Article 5
AI practices mentioned in Article 5 represent specific prohibitive actions that the European Data Protection Supervisor monitors to ensure compliance with regulations.

Data Protection Supervisor
The Data Protection Supervisor is an organization responsible for overseeing the protection of personal data and business secrets.

Litigation or Judicial Proceedings
Litigation or Judicial Proceedings refer to the legal actions initiated by the European Data Protection Supervisor as part of its enforcement activities.

Fines
Fines are monetary penalties imposed as a consequence of certain actions or violations, which must be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive according to the Article.<SEP>Fines are monetary penalties imposed for non-compliance with regulations, including those related to AI model provisions.<SEP>Fines refer to monetary penalties imposed on individuals or organizations for non-compliance with data protection regulations.

Legitimate Interest
Legitimate Interest is a legal basis under data protection laws that allows for the processing of personal data when it serves a legitimate purpose.

General Budget of the Union
The General Budget of the Union is the financial framework within which funds, including those from imposed fines, are managed and allocated.

Relevant Competent Authority
A relevant competent authority is a regulatory body that oversees the compliance and safety of high-risk AI systems, intervening to enforce regulations if necessary.<SEP>Relevant Competent Authorities are regulatory bodies that supervise and enforce compliance of high-risk AI systems to ensure safety and conformity.

Article 16 & 23 Regulation
Article 16 and 23 outline the obligations and responsibilities of providers and importers for high-risk AI systems under European regulations.

Article 23(3)
Article 23(3) sets forth additional compliance obligations for entities involved with high-risk AI systems.

Competent Authority
A competent authority is an entity that has the power to request information from providers of high-risk AI systems to ensure compliance with regulations.<SEP>A competent authority is an organization responsible for overseeing compliance with regulations, particularly in relation to high-risk AI systems.<SEP>Competent Authorities are designated bodies responsible for enforcing compliance and safety regulations concerning high-risk AI systems.<SEP>Competent authorities are regulatory bodies responsible for overseeing compliance and safety standards for high-risk AI systems and addressing non-compliance issues.

real-time remote biometric identification systems
Real-time remote biometric identification systems are advanced technologies used in law enforcement to identify individuals based on biometric data.<SEP>Real-time remote biometric identification systems are technological solutions used in public spaces to identify individuals through biometric data for law enforcement purposes.<SEP>Real-time remote biometric identification systems are technologies used for identifying individuals in publicly accessible spaces, primarily for law enforcement purposes.

criminal offences
Criminal offences refer to legally defined acts that are punishable by law, with a focus on serious crimes as defined in the annex to Regulation.

missing persons
Missing persons are individuals whose whereabouts are unknown, often prompting law enforcement searches based on public interest and safety.

victims of crime
Victims of crime are individuals who have suffered harm due to criminal acts, such as theft, assault, or other offenses, and may require law enforcement assistance for recovery and justice.

terrorist attack
A terrorist attack involves unlawful acts intended to intimidate or coerce a population or government, prompting law enforcement responses to threats.

custodial sentence
A custodial sentence is a court-ordered penalty involving confinement in a prison or similar facility due to serious criminal offenses.

detention order
A detention order is a legal authorization to hold a person in custody, usually related to law enforcement actions following serious crimes.

Council Framework Decision 2002/584/JHA
Council Framework Decision 2002/584/JHA establishes the European arrest warrant and outlines surrender procedures between Member States.<SEP>This event outlines the European arrest warrant and the processes of surrender between Member States, emphasizing cooperation in law enforcement.<SEP>This refers to a legislative framework in the European Union that outlines provisions for cooperation in criminal matters among Member States.

Article 2 of Directive (EU) 2022/2557
Article 2 of Directive (EU) 2022/2557 provides definitions and guidelines pertaining to critical infrastructure and associated threats.

Article 2, point (4) of Directive (EU) 2022/2557
Article 2, point (4) of Directive (EU) 2022/2557 defines critical infrastructure and outlines its importance for public safety and order.

Council Directive 2008/114/EC
This directive focused on the protection of critical infrastructure in the European Union prior to being repealed by Directive (EU) 2022/2557.

Crime
Crime refers to actions that are violations of laws and can involve individuals who may hide their identity from authorities for various reasons.

European Arrest Warrant
The European Arrest Warrant is a legal framework that enables the extradition of criminal suspects between EU Member States, part of the Council Framework Decision 2002/584/JHA.

Competence and Resource Requirements
Competence and resource requirements pertain to the necessary qualifications, skills, and infrastructures needed for national competent authorities to perform their tasks effectively.

Electronic Communication Means
Electronic communication means are the methods by which Member States must publicly share the contact information of competent authorities and single points of contact.

national competent authorities
National competent authorities are designated bodies within Member States responsible for ensuring the compliance of AI systems with established standards.<SEP>National competent authorities are designated governmental bodies within individual EU member states that are responsible for overseeing the implementation and enforcement of regulations related to artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. Their primary role involves ensuring compliance with established standards in cybersecurity and personal data protection, especially concerning high-risk AI systems. Additionally, these authorities are tasked with enforcing compliance with EU regulations and may issue penalties for regulatory infringements. In summary, national competent authorities play a crucial role in maintaining regulatory standards and ensuring that AI models comply with Union law across the member states.<SEP>National competent authorities are responsible for enforcing regulations and notifying bodies under the specified Regulation.

Health and Safety Risks
Health and Safety Risks refer to potential dangers that can arise from the use of AI technologies and requires evaluation by competent authorities.<SEP>Health and safety risks pertain to potential dangers and negative outcomes that can arise from the deployment of high-risk AI systems, necessitating thorough risk assessments.

Member States Reporting
Member States Reporting is the process where EU member states evaluate and report on their national competent authorities' resources and adequacy regarding AI regulation.

2005 Regulation
The 2005 Regulation refers to the legislative framework established for the oversight of AI technologies and their impact on personal data protection and cybersecurity.

AI-on-demand platform
The AI-on-demand platform is an initiative aimed at supporting the implementation of AI technologies through technical and scientific assistance to providers.<SEP>The AI-on-demand platform is an organization focused on promoting and protecting innovation within the framework of Union funding programmes.

European Digital Innovation Hubs
European Digital Innovation Hubs are centers designed to aid businesses, primarily SMEs and start-ups, in leveraging digital technologies.<SEP>European Digital Innovation Hubs are institutions aimed at supporting businesses in digital transformation and compliance with regulatory standards in AI.<SEP>European Digital Innovation Hubs provide support and resources for innovation in digital technologies, including AI, to foster growth and compliance with regulations.<SEP>European Digital Innovation Hubs are entities designed to support the digital transformation of businesses and public sectors by facilitating access to digital technologies, training, and data resources.

Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs)
SMEs are businesses whose interests and needs are taken into account when developing AI governance frameworks.<SEP>Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) refer to smaller businesses that face specific challenges in complying with regulations and accessing expertise in the market.<SEP>SMEs include small and medium-sized businesses that benefit from reduced barriers to access markets through AI regulatory sandboxes, fostering innovation and development in AI.<SEP>Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) are businesses that are targeted by the regulation to support innovation in the AI sector.

EU declaration of conformity
The EU declaration of conformity is a formal document that certifies high-risk AI systems comply with established legal requirements and must be maintained for 10 years.

Annex V
Annex V is an attachment to regulations that contains specific information regarding compliance requirements and the EU declaration of conformity.<SEP>Annex V outlines specific requirements for the EU declaration of conformity, detailing necessary compliance information for high-risk AI systems.

Data Governance and Management Practices
Data governance and management practices are essential for ensuring the quality and appropriateness of data sets used in high-risk AI systems.<SEP>Data governance and management practices comprise strategies and protocols for managing data assets to ensure quality, compliance, and protection against bias and errors in AI systems.

Training Data Sets
Training data sets are collections of data used to train AI models, ensuring they can make accurate predictions or decisions.<SEP>Training data sets are crucial for AI model development, but they can be susceptible to data poisoning attacks.

Validation Data Sets
Validation data sets are used to tune model parameters and assess the performance of AI systems during development.

Testing Data Sets
Testing data sets evaluate the final model's effectiveness before deployment, ensuring its reliability and accuracy.

Data Quality Criteria
Data quality criteria are standards set to ensure that the data used in AI systems is accurate, complete, and free of bias.

Bias Detection Measures
Bias detection measures are practices applied to identify and mitigate biases that may affect AI system outputs and subsequent decision-making.

Geographical Context
Geographical context entails the specific location-related factors that need to be considered in AI data sets.<SEP>Geographical context relates to the specific location characteristics that must be taken into account when designing high-risk AI systems.

EU 2016/679
Regulation (EU) 2016/679 is a legislative framework that establishes data protection and privacy rights within the European Union.

EU 2018/1725
Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 relates to the protection of personal data processed in relation to the European Union institutions.

Directive EU 2016/680
Directive (EU) 2016/680 is designed to protect individuals concerning the processing of personal data by competent authorities for criminal matters.

Data Gaps
Data gaps refer to the missing or insufficient data that affect compliance with regulations, particularly in the context of high-risk AI systems.

Training Datasets
Training datasets are collections of data used to train AI systems, which must be relevant, representative, and error-free.

Validation Datasets
Validation datasets are utilized to validate the performance and accuracy of AI systems during development.

Testing Datasets
Testing datasets are employed to evaluate the effectiveness and reliability of AI systems after their deployment.

Statistical Properties
Statistical properties are the characteristics of data that determine its reliability and usability for AI training and evaluation.<SEP>Statistical properties refer to the characteristics of data sets that determine their representativeness and reliability for training AI systems.

Bias Detection
Bias detection refers to identifying and correcting biases in AI systems to ensure fair outcomes for individuals.

Pseudonymisation
Pseudonymisation is a data management process that replaces identifiable information in a dataset with artificial identifiers to protect privacy.<SEP>Pseudonymisation is a data management process that replaces personally identifiable information with unique identifiers to enhance privacy.

Bias Detection and Correction
Bias detection and correction involve identifying and mitigating biases in AI systems to ensure fair treatment of individuals.<SEP>Bias detection and correction refers to the methods and practices involved in identifying and rectifying biases in data, especially in the context of processing personal data to ensure fairness and accuracy.

Technical Limitations
Technical limitations refer to constraints that hinder the effective use or re-use of personal data, particularly in ensuring security and privacy.

Security and Privacy-Preserving Measures
Security and privacy-preserving measures are protocols established to protect personal data from unauthorized access and misuse during processing.

Records of Processing Activities
Records of processing activities constitute documentation that outlines how personal data is handled, including purposes and compliance with regulatory requirements.

Decision No 768/2008/EC
Decision No 768/2008/EC establishes a common framework for the marketing of products and is key in regulatory compliance.<SEP>Decision No 768/2008/EC is a part of the New Legislative Framework, outlining requirements for the placing on the market and conformity assessment of products.<SEP>This decision provides a common framework for the marketing of products in the EU, establishing compliance criteria.

Council Directive 85/374/EEC
Council Directive 85/374/EEC addresses product liability, ensuring that consumers have rights and remedies in case of damages related to defective products, including AI systems.<SEP>Council Directive 85/374/EEC is a legislative document concerning the liability for defective products in the European Union.<SEP>Council Directive 85/374/EEC pertains to liability for defective products, influencing consumer protection laws in EU member states.

National Labour Law
National Labour Law consists of regulations that govern employment relationships, including working conditions and employee rights within member states.

UNCRC General
The UNCRC (United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child) provides guidelines on the rights of children, which influence laws concerning the protection of minors in the EU.

data.content:
Health and Safety at Work Regulation

Risk-Management Framework
A framework outlined in the regulation to manage risks associated with AI systems and their integration into large platforms and search engines.

data.content:
Interinstitutional Agreement of 13 April 2016 on Better Law-Making
The Interinstitutional Agreement aims to improve the quality of legislation and ensure better law-making processes across EU institutions.<SEP>This agreement lays down principles for cooperation among the EU institutions on legislation and law-making processes aimed at improving regulatory quality.<SEP>This is an agreement aimed at improving the legislative process within the European Union, focusing on effective decision-making.

Article 290 TFEU
Article 290 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union provides the legal basis for the delegation of powers to the European Commission regarding the adoption of certain legislative acts and decisions.

Council
The Council, formally known as the Council of the European Union or the Council of Ministers, is a vital institution within the European Union (EU) framework. It represents the governments of EU member states and plays a key role in the legislative process in collaboration with the European Parliament. The Council is responsible for discussing and adopting laws, as well as making decisions on a variety of policies and regulations.

In addition to its legislative functions, the Council is actively engaged in the development of regulations concerning artificial intelligence (AI). It considers reports and potential amendments related to AI, working closely with the European Commission and the European Parliament to evaluate proposals. The Council has the authority to receive pertinent documents simultaneously alongside experts from member states and participates in Commission expert group meetings related to delegated acts.

Overall, the Council's function as a decision-making body is essential for facilitating discussions among national ministers and contributing significantly to the legislative and policy development on crucial issues, including cybersecurity and AI regulations.

Member States Experts
Member States’ Experts refer to individuals or teams representing Member States who are involved in discussions and expert groups related to the preparation of delegated acts.

Commission Expert Groups
Commission Expert Groups are meetings organized by the Commission where experts discuss and prepare delegated acts.

AI Systems Providers
AI systems providers are entities or businesses that develop and supply artificial intelligence systems and technologies.

AI Systems Deployers
AI systems deployers are organizations or individuals that utilize AI systems, ensuring that they comply with established regulations.

Deployers of AI Systems
Deployers of AI Systems are entities or individuals responsible for implementing AI solutions, obligated to comply with various regulations including transparency.<SEP>Deployers of AI Systems are individuals or organizations that implement artificial intelligence technologies within the Union, adhering to regulatory requirements.<SEP>Deployers of AI systems are organizations or individuals who utilize AI technologies in various applications and must adhere to established codes of conduct.<SEP>Deployers of AI Systems refers to entities or organizations responsible for implementing and managing artificial intelligence technologies and their compliance with regulations.

Article 2(1)
Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 outlines the definitions and scope of economic operators as understood under this regulation.

Article 34(4)
Article 34(4) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 describes the reporting obligations for market surveillance authorities regarding the enforcement of the regulation.

Union Law on Competition Rules
Union Law on Competition Rules refers to the legal framework governing competition and market practices in the European Union.

European Central Bank
The European Central Bank (ECB) is a pivotal institution that serves as the central bank for the euro and is primarily responsible for administering monetary policy within the Eurozone. Its core functions include overseeing the monetary policy of the Eurozone and ensuring financial stability by supervising banking practices and credit institutions. Additionally, the ECB coordinates its efforts with national authorities to effectively manage and implement these policies. Through its responsibilities, the ECB plays a crucial role in maintaining economic stability within the European Union.

Directive 2013/36/EU
Directive 2013/36/EU is a comprehensive European regulation that governs access to the activities of credit institutions and establishes a framework for their prudential supervision within the European Union. This directive outlines essential regulations concerning the governance and risk management of credit institutions, aiming to ensure financial stability within the EU. It pertains not only to credit institutions but also extends to the activities of investment firms, emphasizing the importance of effective supervision. By setting forth requirements for these entities, Directive 2013/36/EU plays a vital role in underpinning the integrity of EU financial frameworks and promoting sound risk management practices among credit institutions.

Single Supervisory Mechanism
The Single Supervisory Mechanism is a system established to ensure effective supervision of credit institutions in the Eurozone under the European Central Bank's oversight.<SEP>The Single Supervisory Mechanism is a system of banking supervision in the Eurozone, designed to ensure the safety and soundness of credit institutions.<SEP>The Single Supervisory Mechanism is a system for banking supervision in the Eurozone, ensuring consistent supervision across participating countries.<SEP>The Single Supervisory Mechanism is a system of banking supervision for the Eurozone, established to ensure the safety and soundness of financial institutions.

High-Risk AI Systems (Annex III)
High-Risk AI Systems listed in Annex III are defined as AI technologies that require stringent regulatory oversight due to their significant impact on safety or fundamental rights.

Regulation (EU) No 1024/2013
Regulation (EU) No 1024/2013 establishes the Single Supervisory Mechanism for banking oversight within the Eurozone.<SEP>Regulation (EU) No 1024/2013 establishes the framework for the Single Supervisory Mechanism in the EU, focusing on banking supervision.

Directive (EU) 2016/679
Directive (EU) 2016/679 is a regulation in EU law on data protection and privacy that establishes protocols for processing personal data.<SEP>Directive (EU) 2016/679, also known as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), is a comprehensive data protection law in the EU that sets guidelines for the collection and processing of personal information.
